Both components reduce portfolio volatility when used to lower beta exposure; however, only the stock-specific (residual) component is associated with a meaningful return premium. In contrast, the industry component, while effective for risk reduction, offers little or no compensation in terms of excess return. This distinction refines our understanding of beta as a risk factor and offers practical implications for asset pricing and portfolio construction. The results highlight the value of disentangling systematic risk into its underlying sources in order to more effectively interpret and exploit the low beta anomaly.

title: Understanding the Motives Behind Steward Ownership: The Ring-Modell
affiliations: Bielefeld University and Bielefeld University

detail.title: Understanding the Motives Behind Steward Ownership: The Ring-Modell

declarations.funderStatement: The authors have not received funding to conduct the research presented.

contentType.other: English summary of a paper published in German

detail.abstract: Why should young founders and established entrepreneurs adopt a structure that prevents them from accessing their companies’ profits, allowing them only to take home a fair salary?  What might sound strange is called steward ownership, a concept that may be described as the opposite of shareholder value orientation and that is attracting significant attention in Germany and worldwide. This paper summarises an interview study that examined the motives and ideas of these pioneers. The original study is published in German as Nina Berenbrinker, Anne Sanders, Christina Hoon, “Ziele und Gründe für Unternehmen mit gebundenem Vermögen: Ring-Modell” Der Betrieb 78 (2025) Issue 42, October 13th 2025, pp. 2552-2561.

title: When Supply Becomes a Demand Signal: Evidence from UK Gilt Issuance

detail.title: When Supply Becomes a Demand Signal: Evidence from UK Gilt Issuance
detail.abstract: For decades, research on sovereign-debt issuance has centred on whether uniform or discriminatory-price auctions best minimise government borrowing costs. This paper argues that the debate may have overlooked subtle design features that can meaningfully affect outcomes. I study the United Kingdom's Post-Auction Option Facility (PAOF)-introduced in 2009-which allows the Debt Management Office, after observing the bid book, to decide whether to activate the facility and sell an additional tranche to winners at the average accepted price. Using the universe of gilt auctions from 1998 to 2017, I find three main results. First, primary dealers bid more aggressively after the PAOF's introduction. Second, the mechanism reduced total fiscal cost by roughly £1.2 billion. Third, the DMO's activation decision-announced with results-moves secondary prices in opposite directions: activation raises prices (lowers yields), while non-activation depresses them, consistent with the model's signaling channel. Together, these findings show that even small, responsive-issuance mechanisms can enhance information revelation and materially lower sovereign borrowing costs without altering the core auction design.

title: Measuring Carbon Risk Dynamics
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business, Blockchain Research Center Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: Measuring Carbon Risk Dynamics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interests.

detail.abstract: Competing asset-pricing theories offer divergent views on carbon risk: risk-based models predict higher returns for carbon-intensive firms, whereas preference-based models imply outperformance of low-carbon assets due to investor reallocation. We develop a Carbon Risk Dynamic Indicator (CARDI) to capture systemic, time-varying carbon risk by predicting relative tail-event measures between high-and low-carbon firms. Our framework shows that rising CARDI strengthens green-asset demand and weakens the traditional high-risk-high-return pattern. Using Chinese daily market data from 2014-2025, we show that CARDI forecasts a time-varying low-carbon premium, providing a tractable tool for incorporating climate-related financial risks into asset-pricing and investment decisions.

title: The Sen-Okun Model: Economic Resilience as a Structural Modifier of Okun's Law

detail.title: The Sen-Okun Model: Economic Resilience as a Structural Modifier of Okun's Law
detail.abstract: Okun's Law-relating GDP growth to changes in unemployment-captures a central macroeconomic regularity but omits structural heterogeneity across economies. I introduce the Sen-Okun Model, a structural formulation that makes the Okun elasticity endogenous to a measurable Sen Composite Resilience Index (SCRI). SCRI aggregates energy resilience, innovation intensity, human capital, and green-transition readiness into a bounded index R ∈ [0, 1]. The model provides analytical expressions for the marginal effect of growth on unemployment as a function of R, derives comparative statics, and characterises identification strategies for empirical implementation. I provide a concrete construction of SCRI (normalisation and weighting rules), a set of testable hypotheses, an identification roadmap (lagging, IV, DiD), and a reproducible simulation recipe in the appendix. The Sen-Okun Model reframes the policy question from "Does growth create jobs?" to "Under what structural conditions does growth create jobs most effectively?

title: It Takes Two: Gender Differences in Group Work *

detail.title: It Takes Two: Gender Differences in Group Work *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study has received ethics approval by the Harvard IRB.
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This study tests for gender differences in credit claimed for individual contributions to group work. I introduce a novel experimental design in which two subjects work together on solving a computerized puzzle, by making alternating moves. Participants play nine rounds, each time with a new partner and puzzle. After each puzzle, they are asked to estimate their contributions towards the solution in incentivized questions. There are no gender differences in ability: women and men are equally good at solving the puzzle both individually and in teams. Despite their equal contribution, women consistently claim less credit than men. This effect is strongest among high contributing women, and women in groups that implemented more complex solutions. I also explore the propensity of participants to undo a partner's move, and I find that men are more likely to correct a partner when he or she made a move that was wrong. These results suggest that gender differences in claiming credit may contribute to the labor market gender gap.

title: Does FDI enhance provincial productivity? A panel data analysis in Vietnam
affiliations: Duy Tan University

detail.title: Does FDI enhance provincial productivity? A panel data analysis in Vietnam

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is funded by Vietnam National Foundation for Science and Technology Development (NAFOSTED) under grant number 502.01-2019.318

detail.abstract: In the present study, we examine foreign direct investment (FDI)- induced productivity spillovers across 60 Vietnamese provinces from 2000 to 2016. Using a generalized method of moments technique, we find that foreign presence has a positive direct effect on total factor productivity (TFP). Furthermore, we discern a positive association between industrial linkages and productivity spillovers. All these findings remain robust to alternative model specifications. After accounting for the roles of human capital in the FDI–TFP nexus, we find absorptive capacity, as measured by human capital, to be a key factor influencing the nature of the foreign presence–productivity spillover nexus in the host province. Specifically, we observe that better human capital enables provinces to better internalize productivity spillovers from foreign presence. This result lends support to the view that human capital must surpass a critical threshold before the host can realize any productivity spillovers engendered by foreign presence.

title: The Hayekian case for wage flexibility in an AI economy

detail.title: The Hayekian case for wage flexibility in an AI economy
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is a shock to labor supply. The emerging policy response wants a small number of large adjustments (e.g. social insurance, regulation, macro policy). A feature of this is that the information requirements are small, e.g. a few high-quality expert reports and plans. But AI applications and labor are both highly heterogeneous, and dynamically so. Those reports and plans will arrive parochial and dated and be useless to everyone except consultants, politicians and journalists. In practice, economic adaptation will require a large number of small adjustments, requiring a flow of information reflecting specific conditions and local trade-offs. Hayek (1945, 1948, 1968) long-ago explained that this is the role of prices and the role of competition is to generate those prices. If the global economy is to adapt to the massive AI shock it needs competition and flexible prices in labor markets to discover where human labor retains and loses value in an AI economy and to communicate that information simply and widely. The rigid wage structures of industrial modernity prevent this price discovery and therefore prevent fast effective economic adaptation to this unprecedented looming shock.

title: Anti-ESG Policy Spillovers: Evidence from US Public Pension Funds
affiliations: University of Bath, School of Management, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU)

detail.title: Anti-ESG Policy Spillovers: Evidence from US Public Pension Funds
detail.abstract: A growing political backlash against sustainable investing has prompted many U.S. states to enact anti-ESG laws restricting public funds from considering ESG factors. We examine how such legislation in implementing states shape the ESG practices of firms headquartered elsewhere through ownership networks of state pension funds. We find firms with greater exposure to affected pensions experience significant declines in ESG performance, even when headquartered outside the enacting states. These declines arise through both exit and voice channels, and are more pronounced in Republican-leaning states. Financial markets respond asymmetrically: low-ESG firms earn positive announcement-window returns, whereas high-ESG firms show muted reactions. Treated firms also report modest improvements in accounting performance. Overall, our evidence shows that anti-ESG policies can propagate across state borders through capital market linkages.

title: Hedge Fund Activism and Value Creation in Family Firms
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Greensboro - Department of Accounting and Finance and James Madison University - College of Business

detail.title: Hedge Fund Activism and Value Creation in Family Firms
detail.abstract: The presence of controlling family owners presents both challenges and opportunities for activist hedge funds. On the one hand, family firms are less likely to be targeted, reflecting the higher intervention costs associated with entrenched control structures. On the other hand, once these barriers are overcome, activists can unlock considerable value in family firm targets. Event study analyses reveal that stock market reacts more positively to activist campaign announcements involving family firms, suggesting greater investor optimism. Triple-difference estimates further show that hedge fund interventions generate greater improvements in family firm targets. Key channels through which activists create value include enhancing operational performance, increasing the likelihood of takeovers, and improving information transparency. Taken together, the evidence highlights the important governance role that activist hedge funds can play in protecting minority shareholder interests and unlocking value in family-controlled firms.

title: Demystifying Cheap Sustainability Talks: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: Singapore Management University and Bayes Business School

detail.title: Demystifying Cheap Sustainability Talks: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: We show that even when firms' sustainability claims are costless and non-verifiable, they can still retain (partial) credibility. Non-babbling equilibria arise in a standard cheap-talk model when investors face uncertainty about both cash flows and the sustainability attribute. In such equilibria, sustainability claims are endogenously negatively correlated with cash flows and positively correlated with the sustainability attribute, even if the two are ex ante independent. The negative cash-flow implication of a claim serves as an endogenous cost, enabling credible communication. We characterize how disclosure behavior and credibility vary with the level of cash-flow uncertainty and provide novel empirical evidence supporting this mechanism. Our results shed new light on firms' communication of sustainability information in the absence of regulatory interventions.

title: Reconciliating Utilitarian Sustainability and Precautionary Principle: The Role of Moral Agency Delegation
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Reconciliating Utilitarian Sustainability and Precautionary Principle: The Role of Moral Agency Delegation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. There are no personal, financial, or institutional relationships that could be perceived to influence the content or conclusions of this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding. The research, analysis, and writing were conducted independently without financial support from any organization, institution, or grant.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that it is possible to reconcile utilitarian sustainability and the precautionary principle by clarifying the role of moral agency. The argument is based on three hypotheses. The "lunatic partner hypothesis" claims that utilitarian sustainability demands knowledge exceeding any individual possibility. The "indeterminate intention-utilitarianism hypothesis" argues that decision-makers can estimate the choice maximising intertemporal welfare, but agents may reach inconceivable solutions and expectations may diverge from reality. The delegation principle emerges when moral agency is denied due to highly biased expectations. It commands delegating the decision to a qualified moral agent or letting such an agency emerge if there is none. The "concealability hypothesis" claims that the acceptable error for moral agency assignment is as low as the matter in question refers to severe and irreversible damages. The paper argues that, when there is no qualified moral agency due to uncertainty and substantial risks, the delegation principle aligns with the precautionary principle and advocates for cost-effective protective actions to secure the emergence of capable and informed moral agents.

title: A Simple Robust Mean-Variance Allocation Theorem for a Single Risky Asset
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Simple Robust Mean-Variance Allocation Theorem for a Single Risky Asset
detail.abstract: We study a one-period portfolio choice problem with a risk-free asset and a single risky asset under mean-variance preferences. The investor faces parameter uncertainty: the expected return of the risky asset is only known to exceed a lower bound, and its variance is only known to be bounded above. We formulate a robust optimization problem in which the investor maximizes the worst-case mean-variance utility over a rectangular uncertainty set. We show that the worst-case parameters lie on the boundary of the uncertainty set, and that the resulting robust allocation problem admits an explicit closed-form solution. The robust optimal weight on the risky asset is obtained by truncating a simple unconstrained fraction, which depends solely on the pessimistic Sharpe ratio and the risk aversion parameter.

title: Forecasting Intraday Trading Volume with Periodicity
affiliations: School of Economics, Jinan University,  Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Jinan University - College of Economics

detail.title: Forecasting Intraday Trading Volume with Periodicity
detail.abstract: We develop the Separated Periodic AutoRegressive (SPAR) model for forecasting intraday trading volume, illustrating its potential as a general framework for modeling periodic patterns without pre-specifying functional forms. Our approach treats intraday periodicity as a time-of-day fixed effect and eliminates it via the standard within-transformation. The out-of-sample results indicate that SPAR significantly outperforms standard benchmarks across various assets and market conditions. Beyond forecasting, SPAR yields an assetspecific intraday periodic curve, and a factor analysis of these estimated curves reveals that volume patterns are primarily driven by two common factors: a U-shaped curve and a morning-afternoon asymmetry. Finally, we apply the SPAR model to a dynamic Volume-Weighted-Average-Price (VWAP) replication strategy, where our forecasts reduce tracking error, underscoring the model's value for algorithmic execution and transaction-cost minimization.

title: Social Capital in Code: Reputation and Heterogeneity in DAO Governance
affiliations: , , The University of Hong Kong - Department of Finance and HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Social Capital in Code: Reputation and Heterogeneity in DAO Governance
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the composition of governance participants shapes financing outcomes in decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). Using a novel dataset that links on-chain voting activity from Snapshot and Tally with off-chain community engagement from Discourse and protocol-level financial data, we construct indices of governance reputation and participant heterogeneity for 92 DAOs between 2020 and 2025. We find that proposals supported by higher-reputation and more diverse governance groups experience significantly stronger post-proposal financing responses, including higher TVL growth, larger capital inflows, and improved token performance, while concentrated voting power predicts weaker outcomes. Mechanism tests show that these effects operate through both a trust channel-where reputable participants stimulate greater community engagement-and a narrative channel-where influential actors attract external attention through social media and search activity. The results indicate that DAO governance serves not only as a decisionmaking mechanism but also as an economically meaningful signal that shapes investor expectations and capital allocation.

title: Applications of Time Series Analysis in Quantitative Finance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Applications of Time Series Analysis in Quantitative Finance
detail.abstract: Time series analysis is a cornerstone of quantitative finance, underpinning models for forecasting asset returns, quantifying risk and optimizing portfolios. Classical statistical models such as ARIMA and GARCH, as well as more recent machine learning and deep learning approaches, have all been applied to financial time series. However, realworld financial markets are non-stationary, regime-switching and highly noisy, which makes direct application of textbook models fragile. In this paper we study the applications of time series analysis in quantitative finance from a unified perspective. First, we formalize a task-model mapping that connects major financial tasks (return forecasting, volatility prediction, risk measurement and dynamic portfolio allocation) with appropriate model classes. Second, we propose a simple Regime-Aware Hybrid Forecasting (RAHF) framework that combines linear time series models with nonlinear learners under a latent-regime view of the market. We provide a detailed bias-variance analysis of the hybrid forecast and show that, under mild conditions, hybridization can reduce mean squared forecast error relative to singlemodel baselines. Finally, we provide an empirical protocol template for evaluating time series models in equity markets, including recommended figures and tables that can be instantiated with Python-generated plots in future work.

title: Unlocking the Hidden Pharmaceutical Financing: Resilient R&D Investment and Malleable Selling Expenses
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics and Singapore Management University

detail.title: Unlocking the Hidden Pharmaceutical Financing: Resilient R&D Investment and Malleable Selling Expenses
detail.abstract: Conventional wisdom holds that when firms face adverse shocks to revenues and market valuations, their R&D investment should contract. This paper shows otherwise: innovation can remain remarkably resilient when firms adjust their internal cost structures. Exploiting China's centralized drug procurement (CVBP) reform as an exogenous shock, we find that the policy sharply reduces pharmaceutical firms' revenues and market capitalization. Yet, contrary to concerns that price regulation suppresses long-term innovation, we detect no decline in firms' R&D expenditures or innovation output. The stability in R&D arises from substantial operational restructuring-specifically, a 19.5% reduction in selling expenses-that offsets revenue losses without reliance on external financing such as bond issuance or bank borrowing. Our findings reveal a cost reallocation channel through which firms can buffer R&D from financial stress, challenging the canonical view that innovation is primarily constrained by access to capital.

title: Limits to VAT Self-Enforcement: Role of Network Frictions in Compliance *
affiliations: , Ashoka University, Indian Administrative Service, Govt of India and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Limits to VAT Self-Enforcement: Role of Network Frictions in Compliance *

declarations.ethicsApproval: The project has approval from the IRB at Ashoka University (IRB Reference: 18_21_Gupta). The RCT has been registered on the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0008357).
declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial assistance from J-PAL, CEGIS, and the International Center for Tax and Development (ICTD).

detail.abstract: The Value-Added Tax incentivizes taxpayers to self-enforce compliance within a supply chain. Combining administrative tax data and a randomized experiment in New Delhi nudging on-time payment, we show that the same incentives that create positive compliance spillovers can constrain enforcement when suppliers are delinquent, because influencing supplier behavior is costly. While nudges increase compliance by 8 percent on average, only taxpayers with high compliance in their supplier network respond. Taxpayers file on time, yet lower net tax payments and continue buying from delinquent suppliers. Our findings highlight how the effectiveness and distributional burden of enforcement depends on production networks.

title: Cybersecurity and Data Protection in Financial Systems: A Comparative Study of Challenges and Regulatory Responses in Developed, Developing, and Emerging Economies
affiliations: Ain Shams University

detail.title: Cybersecurity and Data Protection in Financial Systems: A Comparative Study of Challenges and Regulatory Responses in Developed, Developing, and Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: The global financial sector is undergoing a rapid digital transformation, yet the nature of this shift and its attendant risks vary fundamentally with economic maturity. This paper investigates the challenges and solutions related to cybersecurity and data protection within digital financial systems, applying a comparative analytical lens across developed, developing, and emerging economies. The study reveals that developed economies focus on combating sophisticated cyberattacks and implementing mature, overlapping regulatory frameworks like GDPR and DORA. In contrast, developing economies struggle to secure basic infrastructure and leverage digital identity as a tool for financial inclusion. Meanwhile, emerging economies exhibit rapid FinTech innovation, challenging their regulatory bodies to balance fast-paced growth with systemic stability amidst complex data sovereignty laws. This paper concludes that the "cyber resilience gap" is not merely technological but is fundamentally institutional, legislative, and financial. It recommends a tailored, contextspecific approach to policy rather than a uniform application of international standards, highlighting the role of Regulatory Sandboxes and capacity-building as critical bridges for closing this gap.

title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystems in International British System Schools in Egypt: Transforming Students into Future Innovators
affiliations: Ain Shams University

detail.title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystems in International British System Schools in Egypt: Transforming Students into Future Innovators
detail.abstract: This research examines the integration of entrepreneurial ecosystems within International British System Schools in Egypt. Through analysis of current educational frameworks, global entrepreneurial trends, and Egypt's evolving innovation landscape, the study proposes a comprehensive model for transforming traditional British curriculum schools into hubs of innovation and entrepreneurship. The paper identifies key implementation strategies, including curriculum innovation, industry partnerships, and experiential learning opportunities, aligned with both British educational standards and Egypt's Vision 2030.

title: Do Chaebol Customers Prefer Innovative Suppliers-and What Happens Next?

detail.title: Do Chaebol Customers Prefer Innovative Suppliers-and What Happens Next?
detail.abstract: This study investigates how chaebol firms-large, family-controlled business groups that dominate South Korea's economy-interact with innovative suppliers, both in terms of supplier selection and the subsequent impact on supplier innovation. Drawing on transaction-level data from 2014 to 2019, we find that firms with stronger patent performance are significantly more likely to be selected as chaebol suppliers, suggesting that chaebol firms actively seek out innovation-intensive partners. By implementing a two-stage least squares (2SLS) strategy using industry-level variation in chaebol presence as an instrument, we find a temporary increase in patent quantity following chaebol engagement, but a subsequent decline in patent citation quality, indicating a shift away from high-impact innovation. These findings suggest that while chaebol relationships may initially stimulate innovation activity, they can ultimately suppress long-term or breakthrough innovation due to power imbalances and contractual frictions.

title: Is Delaware Different? Stockholder Lawyering in the Court of Chancery
affiliations: University of Richmond School of Law, University of Michigan Law School and New York University School of Law

detail.title: Is Delaware Different? Stockholder Lawyering in the Court of Chancery
detail.abstract:
Delaware corporate law rests on private enforcement, with stockholder litigation serving as the primary check on managerial misconduct. Delaware judges use attorneys' fees as a lever in these cases to shape the incentives of plaintiffs' counsel. Yet little empirical evidence exists on how Delaware judges exercise their discretion in awarding these fees. Using a hand-collected dataset of stockholder suits filed in the Court of Chancery, this Article provides a systematic analysis of Delaware's fee-award practices. Contrary to Delaware's longstanding judicial assumptions, we find little evidence that fee awards reflect either the risk that these lawyers face when they file contingent cases or the lawyers' performance in these cases. Our data also show that plaintiffs' attorneys receive significantly higher fees in Delaware stockholder cases than in comparable federal securities class actions, despite the similar risk profiles of these cases. The data suggest that current practices may over-reward repeat players and large recoveries while undercompensating smaller claims. 

These findings raise important questions about Delaware's discretionary approach to setting fees. The Delaware judiciary's reliance on broad discretion has produced a system that lacks consistent benchmarks and may reward factors unrelated to risk or performance. Because these awards are ultimately paid from stockholder or corporate funds, the implications extend beyond the bar to Delaware's standing as the preeminent forum for corporate law. The Article outlines several pathways for reform, including enhanced transparency in fee decisions, empirical benchmarking across cases, and multiplier caps to constrain outlier awards. More broadly, the analysis demonstrates how data-driven oversight can strengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of Delaware's system of corporate adjudication. By situating Delaware's approach within the broader landscape of representative litigation, this study also contributes to ongoing debates about the proper calibration of incentives in private enforcement regimes.

title: Integrating Ethos into Resilient Change Facilitation in Ukrainian Realia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hochschule Fresenius - University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Integrating Ethos into Resilient Change Facilitation in Ukrainian Realia
detail.abstract: Purpose. This viewpoint paper explores the practice of change facilitation, aiming to unveil how societies can nurture resilience in the face of imminent challenges. It synthesizes Ukrainian real-life experiences, revealing the principles behind various facilitation approaches to fostering resilient change in demanding contexts. Methodology. The study's methodology entails the synthesis and conceptualization of diverse professional experiences in Ukrainian realia, unravelling the underlying ethos behind various change facilitation approaches. By integrating these insights into broader perspectives and communities of practice, the research aims to offer a holistic perspective on fostering resilient change. Findings. The results section succinctly presents the distilled findings, offering a thought-provoking array of ideas specifically tailored for facilitators operating within high-stakes and extreme-risk and existential environments. Limitations/Implications. Due to the research approach, findings may lack generalizability, necessitating further testing of the presented propositions. Practical Implications. The study concludes by highlighting the potential impact of its professional interpretations on the fields of facilitation and social cohesion. The paper's content encompasses an exploration of facilitation, encompassing Ethos, Logos, and Pathos elements. It highlights the multifaceted role of a facilitator and presents three distinct approaches to implementing change: the knowledge and experience-driven approach, the inspiration-based approach, and the strategy-oriented approach tailored to fragile crisis contexts. Originality/Value. The paper delves into the existential challenges and ethically justified opportunities inherent in adopting the combined approach of facilitation, underlining the nuanced dynamics inherent in resilient change facilitation.

title: Cost matters for micromobility, but so does safety: Investigation of mode choice and induced demand
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM),  and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: Cost matters for micromobility, but so does safety: Investigation of mode choice and induced demand

declarations.funderStatement: This research has been supported by European Union’s Horizon Europe programme under grant agreement No. 101076963 [project PHOEBE (Predictive Approaches for Safer Urban Environment)].

detail.abstract: Emerging micromobility services, such as bike-sharing and e-scooters, are increasingly positioned as sustainable urban transport solutions. Yet, the behavioural role of safety-related attributes remains underexplored, and the concept of induced trips has rarely been investigated. This study makes two key contributions. First, it extends mode choice modelling by explicitly incorporating risk levels and nighttime lighting conditions into multinomial and mixed logit frameworks. Second, and more novel, induced trip models are developed for shared micromobility, employing proportional odds, partial proportional odds, and mixed partial proportional odds formulations. Stated preference data are collected from Athens (Greece), Valencia (Spain), and the West Midlands (UK), marking the first stated-preference investigation of induced micromobility trips. The models are deliberately pragmatic, relying on a parsimonious set of explanatory variables that are transferable across contexts. Two complementary interpretations of the Value of Travel Time (VoTT) are derived: one from conventional mode choice trade-offs and another from travel time and cost reductions affecting induced trips. Results show that poor illumination and higher perceived risk strongly deter micromobility use. For mode choice, West Midlands travellers are most sensitive to out-of-vehicle time, however, exhibit lower VoTT, reflecting local valuation differences. For induced demand, cost and risk primarily influence non-users, while time factors also matter once individuals become users. Scenario analysis reveals that safety improvements generate the largest behavioural shifts, with the probability of choosing car declining, and public transport choice increasing under combined interventions. Overall, safety emerges as a first-order requirement, with cost and time incentives offering complementary benefits.

title: Economic and Structural Determinants of Female Labor Force Participation in South Asia: A Panel Data Approach
affiliations: Shahjalal University of Science & Technology

detail.title: Economic and Structural Determinants of Female Labor Force Participation in South Asia: A Panel Data Approach
detail.abstract: This study analyzes key drivers of female labor force participation (FLFP) in South Asia, utilizing micro-data from the World Bank's Global Labor Database (1990-2022) and crosscountry data from the World Development Indicators (1992-2023). Employing panel data regression models with fixed effects, the study compares various estimation methods to quantify output gains from increased FLFP and assesses the impacts of structural changes, including urbanization, trade openness, and sectoral growth. Key findings reveal that while higher per capita GDP is positively linked to FLFP, a greater share of employment in services shows no significant impact due to skill mismatches and gendered barriers. The analysis highlights that urbanization, although associated with wage premiums for women, also reduces FLFP due to intensified economic constraints. Legal frameworks positively influence FLFP, but the relationship with economic growth follows a U-shaped pattern, while ingrained social norms hinder women's labor participation.

title: From LinkedIn to Labor Statistics: Using Revelio Microdata for Labor Market Research in Developing Economies
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: From LinkedIn to Labor Statistics: Using Revelio Microdata for Labor Market Research in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: We introduce Revelio data—sourced primarily from LinkedIn profiles—as a source of labor force microdata in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where large-sample, high-frequency, employer-linked alternatives are largely unavailable. To address the selection bias inherent to LinkedIn usership, we employ ILO labor statistics to construct weights that correct for non-representativeness across occupations and employer industries. We further validate the weights using national census and Afrobarometer survey data. The weighted dataset then provides a monthly recall panel with comprehensive coverage across Africa, enabling researchers to reliably track micro- and macro-level labor force dynamics since 2008. In addition to linking employees with employers, Revelio offers superior temporal and geographical resolution as well as cross-country comparability, greatly advancing the capacity for labor market research in LMIC contexts.

title: Anti-greenwashing regulation, investor outcomes, and environmental investment: A theoretical approach
affiliations: , University of York and Loughborough University

detail.title: Anti-greenwashing regulation, investor outcomes, and environmental investment: A theoretical approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Freeman is Deputy Chair of the Financial Conduct Authority's independent statutory panel on cost-benefit analysis.

detail.abstract: Recent increased regulatory action against corporate greenwashing is widely expected to improve environmental outcomes and investor welfare. We present a theoretical model which shows that such optimism may be misplaced. Because a regulator is resource-constrained, firm managers have the opportunity to adapt their (mis-)behavior to changes in regulatory focus. Our model presents closed-form solutions for investor portfolio choice under disinformation, managerial behavior that maximizes their own personal compensation under any regulatory regime, and the optimal policy choice for a resource-constrained regulator. We prove that (i) regulators may have little, if any, ability to change investor portfolios and hence the amount of real investment in green projects, (ii) the resulting equilibrium can be non-Pareto optimal for managers, and (iii) regulatory resource is best concentrated in certain areas, which may or may not be the prevention of greenwashing. By showing through this theoretical counterexample that moving regulatory resources into the prevention of greenwashing is not always optimal, the current evidence base is insufficient to give us confidence that the introduction of the International Sustainability Standards Board will necessarily deliver positive outcomes for either investors or the environment.
