title: Documenting debates on GenAI in (reflexive) qualitative research
affiliations: Monash University

detail.title: Documenting debates on GenAI in (reflexive) qualitative research

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a documentation

detail.abstract: This document, as its title indicates, aims to document objectively what happened on the topic of generative AI (genAI) and qualitative research on social media. This starts with the event when Jowsey and colleagues published a LinkedIn post introducing their position statement on rejecting genAI in reflexive qualitative research and calling for endorsement from experienced qualitative researchers. I try to record and present the timeline of related 'events' as they happened. In order to remain relatively objective with my observation, I avoid making my own arguments or reflections on the papers, viewpoints, posts, and responses presented, which I will do in a more formal manner. Rather, I try to present the diversity and nuance of the viewpoints, which come not only from those supporting or opposing the open letter, but also from those in between, including those who are simply observers or learners. In this documentation, while I try to cover as much as I can, there are some responses or posts that are not included here. This may happen because I felt the responses were not adding much value to the discussions or because I was not aware of or missed them. I apologize for this.

title: Revisiting Nike's 2001 Wage Structure and the Feasibility of Living Wages
affiliations: Technical University of Cartagena (UPCT)

detail.title: Revisiting Nike's 2001 Wage Structure and the Feasibility of Living Wages

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Nike's 2001 Corporate Responsibility Report constituted one of the earliest and most detailed wage-transparency disclosures in the global apparel sector. A prior empirical analysis by Martínez (2018) evaluated only 34 countries included in secondary sources, suggesting that Nike could have significantly increased factory wages without jeopardizing profitability. This article presents a replication and methodological extension using the full dataset of 51 countries and 556,722 workers originally reported by Nike. After reconstructing missing wage data using standardized imputation techniques and converting gross wages into total labor costs, we evaluate Nike's wage structure against two internationally recognized poverty thresholds (60 and 150 USD /month). Simulation results reveal that even under conservative assumptions, Nike would have remained highly profitable in 2001 had it doubled or tripled wages for workers earning below these thresholds. Doubling wages in the ten countries below 60 USD /month, for example, would still leave Nike with more than $520 million in net income. These findings reinforce-and substantially strengthen-the conclusions of the 2018 study, demonstrating that living-wage implementation was economically feasible within Nike's historical operating margins. The results contribute to ongoing debates on corporate responsibility, wage justice, and the economic viability of ethical supply-chain practices

title: The Moral Components of Financial Misconduct
affiliations: University of Warwick - Warwick Business School, University of Warwick - Warwick Business School and University of Warwick - Warwick Business School

detail.title: The Moral Components of Financial Misconduct

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was received from University of Warwick: Application Reference HSSREC 163/22-23

detail.abstract: Using a survey experiment we identify four moral components which contribute to the moral unacceptability of financial misconduct. We then use three experiments to test for the presence of scale sensitivity or scale neglect in the manner in which the moral components are judged. We find that the need to lie, or personal communication with the victim both constitute an emotional moral dilemma as they exhibit scale neglect. Whilst colluding with others to effect the misconduct is scale sensitive. So we link financial misconduct via its moral components to the manner in which it will be judged by market participants.

title: From Correlation to Causation: Identifying NATO-Indo-Pacific Cooperation Mechanisms Based on Lossless Knowledge Graphs
affiliations: Dhurakij Pundit University

detail.title: From Correlation to Causation: Identifying NATO-Indo-Pacific Cooperation Mechanisms Based on Lossless Knowledge Graphs
detail.abstract: This study aims to address how NATO can simultaneously advance cooperation and mitigate sensitivities within the Indo-Pacific. The author proposes a three-step approach: guided by the principle of less political discourse and more concrete action (low politicisation and issue-oriented focus), first consolidating standards and collaboration with the Indo-Pacific Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (IP4), then advancing in tiers according to the distinct characteristics of India, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Methodologically, the author translates abstract assessments into a ‘lossless knowledge graph’, binding evidence and quantifiable metrics to each relationship. Visualised data underpins conclusions (e.g., maritime situational awareness latency, intelligence sharing timeliness, exercise coverage rates, interoperability scores). Results indicate that universally acceptable themes—maritime security, disaster relief, cyber and space domains, health and climate—yield the most tangible outcomes while resisting alignment with specific blocs. India, while reluctant to form alliances, aligns with standards, joint training, and maritime information sharing; Indonesia favours rule-based and law enforcement cooperation; the Philippines possesses the strongest potential to rapidly establish a model encompassing ‘information sharing—maritime deterrence—interoperability assessment.’ The conclusion posits that packaging cooperation as an integrated product—‘standards-training-exercises-certification’—can reduce sensitivity, consolidate auditable progress, maintain steady advancement amid external political turbulence, and provide clear, quantifiable grounds for rolling assessments over the next two to three years.

title: Nature Transition Risk
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Finance, , Renmin University of China and Singapore Management University - Lee Kong Chian School of Business

detail.title: Nature Transition Risk
detail.abstract: We investigate how investors assess transition risks arising from the discretionary regulatory mandates for nature conservation. We focus on the UN Biodiversity Conference in Kunming, China, a policy shock signaling heightened political commitment to protection. During the conference, firms exhibited negative abnormal stock returns on average. Using a machine learning approach, we identify historical nature-related subsidies to capture firm-level variations in expectations of mandated conservation engagement, beyond measuring corporate environmental (ecological) impacts. This metric negatively correlates with returns during the conference, particularly for firms with high operational volatility, and those in regions with limited fiscal flexibility and stringent conservation pressures. Investor concerns primarily stem from policy uncertainty, without positive earning expectations from conservation. Our findings underscore the role of authoritative discretion in shaping nature transition risks.

title: Guest Perception and Satisfaction toward the Intimate Concept: A Case Study at Seascape Luxury Resort Sanur
affiliations: Dhyana Pura University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Guest Perception and Satisfaction toward the Intimate Concept: A Case Study at Seascape Luxury Resort Sanur

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent Research
declarations.ethicsApproval: Independent Research
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to analyze the suitability and guest satisfaction levels related to the intimate concept at Seascape Luxury Resort Sanur. Research methods: This study used a quantitative approach through a questionnaire data collection method. The population was all guests at Seascape Luxury Resort Sanur during 2025. The sample was determined as many as 98 guests, using a simple random sampling technique. Data were analyzed using Importance Performance Analysis (IPA) and Customer Satisfaction Index (CSI). Findings: The findings reveal that the implementation of the intimate concept reached a 91.1% suitability level, categorized as very suitable. The Cartesian quadrant analysis indicates comfort as the resort's main strength, while privacy requires improvement. Other aspects contribute positively but are not primary priorities. Guest satisfaction with the intimate concept stands at 69.9%, classified as satisfied. Implications: The findings imply that Seascape Luxury Resort Sanur has successfully implemented the intimate concept, particularly in terms of guest comfort. However, the aspect of privacy still requires improvement through better design and more personalized services. Dimensions such as shared experiences and romantic atmosphere should also be optimized to enhance overall guest satisfaction.

title: Tax Reform and Small Businesses: Strategies for Growth Under Brazil's New IBS/CBS Framework
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research and FUCAPE Business School

detail.title: Tax Reform and Small Businesses: Strategies for Growth Under Brazil's New IBS/CBS Framework
detail.abstract: The Brazilian tax reform, with the implementation of the dual VAT model (IBS/CBS), represents a structural transformation in the consumption tax system, marked by the simplification and unification of taxes. The article analyzes the main changes introduced by the reform, with an emphasis on the impacts for small businesses, both under the Simples Nacional regime and the general regime. Mechanisms such as split payment and full non-cumulative taxation are examined, as well as their repercussions on cash flow, tax credit control, and compliance costs. The study also addresses the operational challenges during the transition period (2026-2033) and proposes adaptation strategies involving financial planning, pricing, technological investment, and professional training. It also highlights the redefinition of the role of accounting, which shifts from a purely fiscal function to an instrument of business intelligence and competitive advantage. It concludes that, although the reform imposes implementation complexities, it offers a unique opportunity for modernization and efficiency gains for companies that anticipate it, converting tax obligations into vectors of sustainable growth.

title: Designing Compensation Contracts for Time-Inconsistent Employees: The Role of Sophistication and Naivety in Goal-Oriented Incentives
affiliations: , Nanjing University, Nanjing University - School of Business, Dongbei University of Finance and Economics and Nanjing University - School of Business

detail.title: Designing Compensation Contracts for Time-Inconsistent Employees: The Role of Sophistication and Naivety in Goal-Oriented Incentives
detail.abstract: Problem definition: We investigate how a firm should design compensation contracts when the employee has timeinconsistent preferences, differentiating between sophisticated types (who correctly anticipate their self-control problems) and naive types (who hold overly optimistic beliefs about their future behavior). Methodology/results: Using a bilevel Stackelberg game framework, we model the strategic interaction between a profit-maximizing firm and a time-inconsistent employee. Our analysis reveals a compelling paradox: while time inconsistency leads to procrastination that reduces the firm's profit, it simultaneously benefits the sophisticated employee through improved contractual terms in a vibrant economy. For a naive employee, we show how her misperception leads to contract acceptance followed by abandonment, creating significant inefficiencies for both parties. We develop and characterize two novel contracting approaches: naivetyresponsive contracts (adjusting to discovered naivety ex post) and naivety-embedded contracts (designed with ex ante awareness of naivety). Managerial implications: Our findings offer valuable insights for managing temporally inconsistent workforces. The firm can benefit from identifying the employee's types and implementing adaptive contracts that account for the employee's present-biased preference. Specifically, in vibrant economies with a high reservation utility, the firm need not invest in costly naivety detection, as market pressures naturally constrain attrition. For a naive employee, naivetyembedded contracts maximize the firm's profit, while naivety-responsive contracts yield better social welfare outcomes. The proposed flexible contracting approach provides the firm with a practical tool for reducing attrition among naive employees while maintaining incentive power, ultimately turning behavioral limitations into productive outcomes.

title: Sentiments about Others in the Stock Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University College London

detail.title: Sentiments about Others in the Stock Markets
detail.abstract: Applying large language models to more than 46 million StockTwits posts, we separate messages expressing an author's own outlook from those describing others' reasoning or expected actions, yielding firm-week measures of subjective sentiment and subjective disagreement. References to others are pervasive and typically more pessimistic than investors' own views. Higher order posting and subjective sentiment vary with disagreement, returns, and valuation. Retail order imbalance increases with investors' own sentiment but decreases with the sentiment they attribute to others, indicating a contrarian response. This contrarian effect is much stronger when subjective and objective sentiment are close and when volatility is high, consistent with investors acting more contrarian when viewing others' beliefs as a less precise signal.

title: The Paradox of Negative Contribution in Scientific Literature: Why Ninety-Five Percent of Journal Articles May Represent Scientific Debt Rather Than Progress
affiliations: Shenyang Normal University

detail.title: The Paradox of Negative Contribution in Scientific Literature: Why Ninety-Five Percent of Journal Articles May Represent Scientific Debt Rather Than Progress
detail.abstract: The scientific publishing landscape has become increasingly dominated by publications that contribute little, or even negatively, to genuine knowledge advancement. While conventional wisdom suggests that approximately 5% of journal articles possess genuine scientific value-with the remaining 95% characterized as incremental contributions-this framing fundamentally misrepresents the problem. This paper argues that the majority of this 95% should be classified as negative contributions: publications that actively retard scientific progress through logical errors, flawed methodologies, and wasted resources. Employing a framework of quantitative analysis, we demonstrate that negative contributions do not accumulate through multiplicative damage but rather through intensification of singular foundational errors. Furthermore, we identify a critical paradox in contemporary science funding: positive contributions increasingly emerge from unfunded research, while the substantial majority of institutional funding supports the proliferation of negative contributions. This creates a perverse ecosystem where breakthrough innovations face funding scarcity while mediocre or erroneous work flourishes under generous financial support, including direct subvention through publication mills and predatory journal systems. The consequences extend beyond wasted resources-they represent a systematic suppression of scientific progress.

title: Allocating the Cost of Town Walls in Medieval Castile: A Rabbinic Analysis
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Allocating the Cost of Town Walls in Medieval Castile: A Rabbinic Analysis
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the normative criteria proposed by Rabbi Maeir Halevi Abulafia (Ramah) for allocating the cost of building urban fortifications among Jewish aljamas in medieval Castile. Using textual and historical-interpretive analyses of rabbinic sources, this paper maintains that Ramah's extensive cost allocation analysis of town walls was driven by historical events surrounding the Reconquista. The paper finds that Ramah's geometric cost allocation scheme is consistent with both Talmudic and economic efficiency reasoning. Because the Talmudic letter of the law conflicted with equity considerations, the Ramah was forced to do an "about face" and rationalize a more equitable approach, if only by reference to less-than-ideal Talmudic sources. This study contributes to the historical accounting/finance literature by showing that cost allocation in medieval Spain was justified both on efficiency and equity grounds-albeit moderated by historical exigencies-in consonance with some of the modern cost allocation literature.

title: Inventory Management and the Cross-section of Stock Returns
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and University of Toronto

detail.title: Inventory Management and the Cross-section of Stock Returns
detail.abstract: We study how firms' inventory policies shape their exposure to aggregate demand and supply shocks. In a production-based asset pricing model with inventory management, we show that the shadow value of inventories reflects two opposing forces: a cost-smoothing channel that hedges adverse supply shocks by allowing firms to sell from inventory when marginal costs rise, and a stock-out option value that amplifies exposure to demand shocks as inventories become less valuable in low-demand states. This duality implies that inventories can act as either a hedge or a source of risk, depending on the shock. Empirically, firms with higher inventories load positively on demand shocks and negatively on supply shocks, and the resulting inventory premium varies with the prices of these risks. Inventories thus play a central role in transmitting fundamental macroeconomic shocks into asset prices.

title: Implications of Brazil's CBS/IBS Tax Reform for Cost Accounting and Management Control
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research and University of São Paulo (USP)

detail.title: Implications of Brazil's CBS/IBS Tax Reform for Cost Accounting and Management Control
detail.abstract: The consumption tax reform in Brazil, consolidated by Constitutional Amendment No. 132/2023 and Complementary Law No. 214/2025, represents a transformative milestone for cost accounting and managerial accounting. By replacing five cumulative taxes with two non-cumulative taxes-the Contribution on Goods and Services (CBS) and the Tax on Goods and Services (IBS)-the Brazilian tax system adopts a dual Value Added Tax (VAT) model, in line with international practices. This article analyzes the impacts of this reform on cost measurement, price formation, and business performance indicators. The results point to the need to reconfigure costing systems, review indirect cost allocation criteria, and integrate the tax, accounting, and management modules. In addition, the challenges of the service sector, which is more exposed to the increase in the effective tax burden, are highlighted. It is concluded that the reform, by eliminating historical distortions and increasing transparency, creates opportunities for more accurate and strategic cost management, but requires a profound adaptation of information systems and management practices.

title: Equal Job, Unequal Pay? Evidence from 4 Million Regulatory Careers
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School, Drexel University and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: Equal Job, Unequal Pay? Evidence from 4 Million Regulatory Careers
detail.abstract: Using a novel dataset covering 36.5 million employee-year observations across 334 government agencies from 1973-2023, we document persistent and widespread gender pay disparities. Women earn 19.8% less than men in raw comparisons. Moreover, women earn 0.8% less when comparing employees within the same local office, occupation, rank, and tenure, which represents a wealth loss of $250,000 by retirement for a representative female employee. This gap arises from women: sorting into lower-paying offices, having lower promotion rates, and having lower pay within-rank. We examine three economic mechanisms. First, the gap is concentrated among higher ranks and more educated employees, consistent with gender gaps in negotiation and subjective evaluation. Second, female leadership mitigates pay gaps for lower-ranked females. Third, labor mobility plays a negligible role.

title: Impact of culture in peer-to-peer lending
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology

detail.title: Impact of culture in peer-to-peer lending
detail.abstract: We document that culture and cultural perception both influence financial decisions. We examine the impact of clan culture, an important dimension of Chinese culture, on individual lending behavior. Using data from RenRenDai, a leading peer-to-peer lending platform in China, we find that borrowers from regions with higher clan culture are more likely to get loans funded, attract larger bids from lenders, get loans funded faster, are less likely to default, and repay a larger fraction of their loans. These effects are more pronounced when there is greater information asymmetry, borrowers are older or from rural areas, and the legal environment is weaker. These results are robust to alternative measures of clan culture. Lenders rely less on culture as a signal of creditworthiness for borrowers with observable default history. Our results suggest that clan culture acts as a substitute for formal institutional mechanisms and participants in the peer-to-peer market use information about clan culture as a proxy for economic factors, improving efficiency of financial decisions.

reference: PENSOS : Jurnal Penelitian dan Pengabdian Pendidikan Sosiologi, Volume 3, No. 2. Pp. 117-138
title: Reasons For the Lack of Acceptance of the New Curriculum 2021 in Bangladesh Among Teachers, Students, and Parents at The Field Level
affiliations: Dhaka Residential Model College

detail.title: Reasons For the Lack of Acceptance of the New Curriculum 2021 in Bangladesh Among Teachers, Students, and Parents at The Field Level

publicationDetails.detailsText: PENSOS : Jurnal Penelitian dan Pengabdian Pendidikan Sosiologi, Volume 3, No. 2. Pp. 117-138

detail.abstract: The introduction of Bangladesh's New Curriculum 2021 a progressive shift from rote learning to competency-based education has faced significant resistance from teachers, students, and parents, undermining its potential to transform the nation's education system. This study identifies the structural, cultural, and logistical barriers driving this resistance, including implementation gaps, urban-rural disparities, inadequate stakeholder involvement, and misaligned assessment practices. Through qualitative analysis of field-level challenges, the research reveals a critical disconnect between policy design and grassroots realities, particularly in resource-constrained rural areas. Teachers struggle with insufficient training and excessive workloads, students grapple with ambiguous evaluation criteria, and parents distrust reforms due to poor communication and financial burdens. The urban-rural divide exacerbates inequities, with rural schools lacking digital infrastructure, trained educators, and basic materials. The study underscores the urgency of collaborative reforms, emphasizing stakeholder engagement, equitable resource distribution, and alignment of assessments with higher education. By addressing these challenges, Bangladesh can bridge the gap between policy aspirations and practical execution, ensuring the curriculum fosters inclusive, future-ready learning.

title: STEM, Skills, and Society: Evaluating Ghana’s Competency-Based Curriculum Reform (2019–2024)
affiliations: Dhaka Residential Model College, Dhaka Residential Model College, Jahangirnagar University - Department of CSE, Char Adarsha College, Kishoreganj, , Dhaka College and Shamplapur Ideal Academy, Bangladesh

detail.title: STEM, Skills, and Society: Evaluating Ghana’s Competency-Based Curriculum Reform (2019–2024)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known personal or financial relationships with any individuals, organizations, or institutions that could have influenced the work reported in this study. All six authors confirm that there are no competing interests or potential conflicts to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Formal ethics approval was not required for this study in accordance with national/institutional guidelines. All participants provided written informed consent prior to their involvement.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no external funding for this research. All work was carried out using the authors’ own resources with no financial support from any organization or institution.

detail.abstract: Ghana’s ambitious curriculum reform places education at the centre of its national development strategy, Ghana Beyond Aid. This paper examines the systemic integration of STEM education, future-ready skills, and societal transformation into the country’s pre-tertiary system. Using a mixed-methods approach including stakeholder interviews, policy analysis, and fieldwork in five regions we explore how Ghana’s 2019 shift to a competency-based curriculum is replacing rote learning to cultivate critical thinkers, digital citizens, and ethical leaders. Findings highlight initiatives to integrate technical STEM skills through coding pilots and local digital resources, alongside pedagogical changes to nurture the 4Cs (critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, communication) and digital literacy. The curriculum is impact-oriented, emphasizing social relevance by promoting gender equality in STEM, creating TVET pathways for informal economies, and incorporating ethics modules on corruption and sustainability. Despite progress, challenges persist, including urban-rural resource imbalances, teacher capacity gaps, and tension between high-stakes examinations and skill assessment. This study suggests Ghana’s triad approach offers a replicable model for other African countries aiming to align education with sustainable development. Long-term success, however, depends on scaling teacher training, strengthening public-private infrastructure partnerships, and connecting global competencies to Ghana’s unique cultural and economic context. This reform is not merely a pedagogical shift, but an investment in human capital for inclusive socio-economic transformation.

title: Disagreement about Monetary Policy and the Equity Term Structure
affiliations: Cleveland State University, Cleveland State University and Cleveland State University

detail.title: Disagreement about Monetary Policy and the Equity Term Structure
detail.abstract: We document that belief disagreement about monetary policy has economically meaningful effects on the term structure of equity yields. We then rationalize these findings by developing a general-equilibrium model, which shows that disagreement about the monetary authority's reaction to inflation deviations increases equity yields, with stronger effects in recessions. Monetary-policy disagreement affects equity yields primarily through its impact on the risk-sharing rule. Taken together, our empirical and theoretical results highlight the importance of agents' disagreement about monetary policy for the pricing of both short-and long-term assets.

title: Advanced Equity Index Tracking: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Models, Stock Selection, and Weighting Strategies over 30 Years
affiliations: Rodex Risk Advisers LLC

detail.title: Advanced Equity Index Tracking: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Models, Stock Selection, and Weighting Strategies over 30 Years

keywords: C61 – Optimization Techniques; Programming Models; Dynamic Analysis
C45 – Neural Networks and Related Topics

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates a range of models for index tracking over a 30-year period, employing a combination of machine learning (ML) methods, simple benchmarks, and an advanced optimisation approach by [1] Benidis et al. (2018). It explores two critical aspects: stock selection and weighting. To this end, this paper presents results of a horse race of several Unsupervised ML methods, i.e., Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC), t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding in combination with Spectral Clustering (t-SNE), Self-Organising Maps (SOM), and Auto-Encoders (AE). An optimisation method recently suggested by [1] Benidis et al. (2018), as well as a plain correlation-based model, and a stratified sampling method round off the field of participants. The stratified sampling method serves as simple but hard to beat benchmark. In total, eight different tracking models are analysed. The methods to select the tracking stocks build on the different ML models and exploit their specific characteristics to accomplish close tracking. The models are analysed based on tracking error, turnover, active returns and risk factor exposure, providing insights into their suitability for closely replicating an index or generating excess returns. The findings highlight Stratified Sampling, the Benidis method and some variants of the SOM as useful for tracking, while ML methods like Auto-Encoders, PCA, t-SNE and SOM demonstrate potential for alpha generation.

title: Disagreement and Stock Liquidity

detail.title: Disagreement and Stock Liquidity
detail.abstract: I empirically investigate how disagreement among investors relates to stock liquidity and why such a relationship exists. I find that when there is disagreement, the adverse selection component of liquidity increases, and the inventory component of liquidity decreases. The relationship between disagreement and liquidity then depends on the relative magnitudes of disagreement's associations with the adverse selection and inventory components. Due to this, I find that the relationship varies across stocks. This finding potentially explains mixed findings in prior studies. To understand why such a relationship exists, I further examine two sources of disagreement, information asymmetry (IA) and differential interpretation (IN). Using a novel empirical design, I evaluate mechanisms through which IA and IN can affect liquidity. Results indicate that the relationship exists because the mechanisms of Easley and O'hara (1992) and Glosten and Milgrom (1985) are more important than Kyle and Wang (1997).

title: The Causal Effect of Trade Unions on Workers’ Health: A Parametric G-Formula Approach Using Longitudinal Data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID)
affiliations: Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), University of Glasgow - MRC/CSO Social and Public Health Sciences Unit and Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB)

detail.title: The Causal Effect of Trade Unions on Workers’ Health: A Parametric G-Formula Approach Using Longitudinal Data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received funding from the following: The Belgian National Fund for Scientific Research (FNRS), Incentive Grant for Scientific Research (MIS), NegHealth – 40021242, beneficiary: Jacques Wels, The Belgian National Fund for Scientific Research (FNRS), Research Associate (CQ), 40010931, beneficiary: Jacques Wels, The UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Guarantee funding for Horizon Europe ERC grant, UHealth – UKRI1426, beneficiary: Jacques Wels.

detail.abstract:
Background: Trade unions are increasingly recognized as public health actors. They both protect workers’ health by ensuring workplace health and safety and, indirectly, by providing economic advantages to their members. However, previous research has not addressed the direct and indirect causal pathways between trade unions and health and only focused on membership, omitting the important role that the presence of trade union has within the workplace.

Methods: We used two decades of nationally representative longitudinal data from the United States (PSID 2001-2021; ≈26,000 individuals; ≈117,000 person-years), used Exploratory Causal Discovery to detect causal pathways and applied parametric g-formula modelling to account for time-varying confounding.

Findings: Sustained union membership was associated with lower psychological distress (Mean Ratio – MR 0.944; 95% CI 0.916–0.974), with a persistent direct effect after adjusting for income, working hours, and housing (MR 0.937; 95% CI 0.907–0.968). Always workplace union presence showed an association (MR 0.972; 95% CI 0.945–0.999) that attenuated after adjusting for mediators. Improvements in self-reported health were primarily mediated by income and working-hours pathways (always union membership total adjust MR 0.991; 95% CI 0.983–1.000; always union presence total adjust: MR 0.990; 95% CI 0.982–0.998).

Interpretation: By examining both union membership and workplace union presence, this study captures the individual and institutional dimensions of unionization that have not been simultaneously addressed in prior research. It highlights the significant role trade unions play in improving workers’ health and the threat the erosion of collective bargaining in the US might pose for population health.

title: You Wouldn't Steal a Car: Moral Intuition for Intellectual Property
affiliations: Samford University and Chapman University - Smith Institute for Political Economy and Philosophy

detail.title: You Wouldn't Steal a Car: Moral Intuition for Intellectual Property
detail.abstract: We conduct an experiment to compare how people respond to the appropriation of rivalrous versus nonrivalrous goods. Analysis of chat transcripts indicates that people use language associated with "stealing" exclusively for rivalrous goods. Moreover, taking rivalrous goods precipitates negative emotional shifts in conversations, while appropriating nonrivalrous goods does not. Even though their work is copied extensively, creators of nonrivalrous goods do not seek intellectual property protection when attribution is assured. These findings help explain why digital piracy in the internet age provokes moral judgments distinct from those involving physical theft. They suggest that our moral evaluations originate more from the rivalrousness of the good than from the act of taking itself and therefore challenge the applicability of intellectual property law frameworks formulated before the advent of widespread digital sharing.

title: Magnitude Effects in Preference Reversals: A Meta-Analysis

detail.title: Magnitude Effects in Preference Reversals: A Meta-Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Preference reversal (PR) occurs when individuals reverse their preferences between safe and risky bets depending on the elicitation method (e.g., direct choice vs. certainty equivalence). Although prior research has rarely examined the influence of relative payoff ratios between bets on choice preferences and PR, this meta-analysis synthesizes data from 22 experiments or treatments across 13 studies, comprising 326 unique scenarios (N = 1,947). The mean effect sizes were close to zero, but substantial heterogeneity emerged across studies. Several idiosyncratic moderators-including probability and payoff structures and design features-appear to shape when choice preferences and PR are more likely to occur.

title: The Chipko Movement: An Ecofeminist Case Study of Environmental Resistance and Social Justice
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: The Chipko Movement: An Ecofeminist Case Study of Environmental Resistance and Social Justice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This paper was prepared independently as part of a Master’s degree assignment at Queen Mary University of London and received no external funding or institutional influence beyond standard academic supervision.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the climate crisis through a critical ecofeminist lens, arguing that this framework is essential for understanding the interconnected oppression of women and nature. Using the Chipko Movement in the Indian Himalayas as a case study, the analysis demonstrates how patriarchal and capitalist systems, rooted in colonial-era policies, drive environmental degradation and social injustice. The paper traces the movement's origins as a direct response by women to commercial forestry that threatened their livelihoods and ecosystems. By hugging trees to prevent felling, Chipko activists championed an ethic of care and reciprocity, directly contesting state-led, profit-driven resource management. The movement's success illustrates the power of grassroots, nonviolent resistance and highlights the crucial leadership of women in environmental activism. Ultimately, this paper posits that achieving climate justice requires integrated solutions that dismantle intersecting systems of oppression and prioritize both ecological integrity and gender equity.

title: Building an Open-Source Barra-Like Specific Return Model

detail.title: Building an Open-Source Barra-Like Specific Return Model
detail.abstract: This working paper outlines how the open-source hornli-hsr project builds a free alternative to Barra's proprietary specific return model. It combines daily market data and quarterly fundamentals to compute standardized descriptors (e.g., size, value, momentum, leverage, volatility) which are then aggregated into style factor exposures. On each trading day, factor returns are estimated via cross-sectional regressions of stock returns on their industry, country and style exposures; specific returns are obtained as residuals and used to build an EWMA covariance estimator. To avoid look-ahead bias, fundamental data are aligned by quarter-end dates and shifted so only information available at the time is used. Factor and specific return series and descriptor-level exposures are released publicly, while raw price and fundamental data remain proprietary. HSR (Hornli Specific Return) is an open-source research tool, not affiliated with or endorsed by MSCI/Barra and not intended as investment advice.

title: The Geography of Enslaved Wealth: How Resource-Rich Lands Produce Poor Societies
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: The Geography of Enslaved Wealth: How Resource-Rich Lands Produce Poor Societies
detail.abstract: This paper explores why regions rich in natural resources often show weak innovation, limited social mobility, and persistently low living standards. By comparing Siberia, Central Asia, and Saudi Arabia, it argues that the main barrier is not geology but political control over capital, trade, and information. The analysis introduces the idea of a “modern iron curtain of investment,” where states restrict foreign direct investment in key sectors to prevent the spread of wage transparency, merit-based management, and civic expectations that come with global companies. At the same time, rentier-state dynamics turn external resource rents into domestic patronage, replacing diversification and productivity-driven growth with subsidies and public employment. The paper places the petrodollar system and current de-dollarization efforts within this framework, suggesting that currency systems influence market access more than resource endowments alone. Methodologically, the study combines historical research with secondary data from UNCTAD, IMF, IEA, and USGS to examine how capital openness, logistics, and governance shape economic outcomes. The main argument is that prosperity depends on awareness and participation, not just resource possession; when investment and knowledge are restricted, resource wealth becomes a political tool instead of a development pathway.

title: Green ports or green paradox? Empirical evidence from Norwegian port municipalities
affiliations: Ph.D., Associate Professor, NTNU, Norway

detail.title: Green ports or green paradox? Empirical evidence from Norwegian port municipalities
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether public investment in green maritime infrastructure and transportation projects contributes to CO₂ emission reductions in Norwegian port municipalities. Using panel data for 28 coastal municipalities from 2016 to 2023, the analysis assesses the temporal effects of maritime-supported projects, technology development (TransMar) and infrastructure (InfraMar), on local maritime emissions. A two-stage empirical strategy combines lagged panel regressions (OLS, FE, and RE) with unsupervised clustering to uncover structural heterogeneity in port activity and investment profiles. The results reveal that transport-related investments exhibit statistically significant emission-reducing effects with lags of three to five years, supporting the long-term decarbonization potential of targeted funding. In contrast, green infrastructure presence correlates positively with emissions, likely reflecting higher port activity and policy targeting in high-emission areas. Clustering analysis confirms that municipalities differ substantially in activity levels, investment patterns, and emission profiles, reinforcing the case for differentiated policy strategies. The findings contribute to environmental economics and maritime policy by offering new microlevel evidence on the effectiveness and temporal dynamics of green investments. This paper extends previous literature by integrating spatial clustering with dynamic investment modeling, providing novel insights into how policy timing and local industrial structure shape emission outcomes. The results have direct implications for designing adaptive, region-specific maritime decarbonization programs and guiding future EUaligned infrastructure strategies.

title: Neural Correlates of Interactions between Adaptive Learning and Hierarchical Reasoning in Repeated Strategic Games
affiliations: Hefei University of Technology, Shanghai International Studies University, South China Normal University, Claude Bernard Lyon 1 University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai International Studies University, Shanghai International Studies University and Claude Bernard Lyon 1 University

detail.title: Neural Correlates of Interactions between Adaptive Learning and Hierarchical Reasoning in Repeated Strategic Games
detail.abstract: Repeated strategic interactions with consistent partners involve both adaptive learning and hierarchical reasoning. Hybrid models that incorporate reasoning into adaptive learning paradigms have been proposed to capture these processes and their interactions at the behavioral level. Here, we employ model-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to investigate the neural computations underlying decisions in repeated strategic interactions between two players using 11-20 money request games. A hybrid model more accurately explains medial prefrontal cortex activity compared with pure adaptive learning models. Additionally, we find that regions such as the rostral anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, right temporoparietal junction, precuneus, and anterior insula correlate with prediction error signals generated by adaptive, simulated adaptive, and sophisticated learning from the hybrid model. Together, our findings provide novel neural-level support for the interplay between adaptive learning and hierarchical reasoning in a repeated game with fixed partners.

title: States, Markets, and Citizens: Rethinking Vietnam’s Development through an AI Lens
affiliations: RMIT University Vietnam and National Taiwan University

detail.title: States, Markets, and Citizens: Rethinking Vietnam’s Development through an AI Lens

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data, and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study leverages artificial intelligence (AI) to revisit Vietnam’s post-Đổi Mới development through an expert-based meta-analysis. Rather than relying on direct interviews—which are often affected by recall or framing bias—we compile and analyze the published works of leading Vietnam scholars, each with at least three Scopus-indexed (Q2 or higher) papers in the past five years and seven across their careers. Using AI-driven content analysis, we synthesize these expert perspectives into a four-pillar framework encompassing the public, private, and civil sectors, and their interlinkages. The results reveal that Vietnam’s transformation is shaped by complex systemic interdependencies: public infrastructure and governance quality act as central enablers, while corruption, coordination failures, and skill mismatches remain major constraints. Methodologically, this study introduces an AI-assisted synthesis approach that bridges qualitative depth with analytical rigor, offering a replicable framework for analyzing other transitional economies.

title: Too Open to Fail? The Impact of Mandated Open Banking on Banks' Systemic Risk across the Globe.
affiliations: , Bangor University, Bangor Business School and

detail.title: Too Open to Fail? The Impact of Mandated Open Banking on Banks' Systemic Risk across the Globe.
detail.abstract: We compile a hand-collected dataset on open banking across 168 countries to provide the first empirical evidence on the impact of mandated open banking regulations on banks’ systemic risk across the globe spanning the period 2013Q1–2024Q4. Employing a staggered difference-in-differences design, the results show that mandated open banking reduces banks’ systemic risk. We identify three non-mutually exclusive channels underlying this effect: (i) increased loan diversification, (ii) reduced information asymmetry, and (iii) enhanced monitoring. We also document that mandated open banking reduces bank-specific risks. We contribute to the ongoing debate on the effect of open banking on global financial stability.

title: Real Estate Investment Funds and Housing Accessibility in Brazil: Balancing Financial Returns with Social Impact
affiliations: Centro Universitário das Américas

detail.title: Real Estate Investment Funds and Housing Accessibility in Brazil: Balancing Financial Returns with Social Impact
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of Real Estate Investment Funds (FIIs) on housing accessibility in Brazil. While FIIs mobilize significant capital and enhance market liquidity, conventional funds focused on commercial and luxury residential properties contribute little to addressing the housing deficit. In contrast, socially oriented FIIs demonstrate the potential to balance financial returns with the provision of affordable housing for middle-income households. Through case illustrations and theoretical analysis of financialization, the research highlights the trade-offs between profitability and social impact. Policy measures, including tax incentives, regulatory guidance, and public-private partnerships, are identified as key mechanisms to redirect FII investments toward inclusive housing. The findings underscore the role of financial markets in shaping social outcomes and provide insights for policymakers, investors, and academics seeking to align investment strategies with broader societal goals.

title: Localizing Climate Action in Cities: Applying Historical Ecology to Urban Climate Governance

detail.title: Localizing Climate Action in Cities: Applying Historical Ecology to Urban Climate Governance
detail.abstract: Cities are at the epicenter of global climate action. As a feature of urban climate governance, several major cities across the United States have developed multi-year action plans to conceptualize and coordinate their climate mitigation and adaptation efforts. For certain cities, these plans have been transformative. Leveraging resources and policy processes, they integrate climate resilience-building into long-term planning and urban development projects. However, the literature and practice of urban climate governance typically exist between the present and the future. There is relatively minimal regard for the historical forces that have shaped regional ecologies and cities, some for hundreds of years. Drawing upon historical ecology approaches, utilizing geoinformatics, and conducting quantitative and qualitative content analysis of city-specific climate action plans, this study examines how and why cities are applying historical knowledge and ecological principles in urban climate governance. The findings indicate that city planners and officials are increasingly integrating ecological practices and historical knowledge systems as a means of localizing, customizing, and better contextualizing climate action, particularly focusing on reducing combined risks in highly susceptible communities and urban landscapes. Green engineering and infrastructure, water resource management, and urban biodiversity enhancement are areas where this application has been most evident. Cities nevertheless encounter significant governance challenges in meeting the desired climate action outcomes. The results suggest that limited availability of historical data, ethical considerations regarding the use of Indigenous knowledge, climate solutions disparities, and historical path dependency are among the main limiting factors.

title: Mobile working vs. labour mobility: a conceptual exploration of substitution and urban change
affiliations: IMC University of Applied Sciences Krems, Munich Business School and IMC University of Applied Sciences Krems

detail.title: Mobile working vs. labour mobility: a conceptual exploration of substitution and urban change
detail.abstract: This paper discusses the impact of remote work on labour mobility and urban development. We argue whether remote work can replace high-skilled migration especially if job opportunities drive migration decisions. Given the characteristics of jobs that are suitable for remote working, along with different cost and types of migration we conclude that remote work is a good substitute for physical migration of high-skilled workers. The analysis highlights that this substitution leads to a relative increase in low-skill migration in urban areas, potentially affect-ing economic and social structures as well as land-use not only in urban areas but also in sub-urban areas. The study emphasizes the need for urban policies to adapt to these changes by promoting inclusive economic development plans and enhancing urban amenities to support a diverse and skilled workforce.

title: Determinants of Warehouse Management Systems (WMS) Implementation By Logistics Service Providers (LSPs) in Malaysia

detail.title: Determinants of Warehouse Management Systems (WMS) Implementation By Logistics Service Providers (LSPs) in Malaysia
detail.abstract: This paper studies the determinant factors that influence the implementation of Warehouse Management Systems (WMS) by Logistics Service Providers (LSPs) in Malaysia. The influencing factors include cost of the technology, compatibility of the technology, organizational readiness, top management support, the size of the organization, competitive pressures and government support. To provide insight into these factors, this study employed a questionnaire survey. The data are obtained from 114 logistics companies. The findings demonstrated that implementing new technologies will improve business performance for Malaysia's logistics sector and that organizational, technological, and environmental factors have a major impact on the implementation of technological breakthroughs.

title: The Role of Universities: Enhancing Students' Capabilities for Work and Life
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Budapest Business School, Students and Hochschule Fresenius - University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: The Role of Universities: Enhancing Students' Capabilities for Work and Life
detail.abstract: This chapter focuses on the role of universities in cultivating students' capabilities to sustain their careers in the changing world of work and to flourish in life through their personal becoming. First, the chapter outlines the ecosystems of universities. Next, it presents the challenges and opportunities society and the world of work pose to universities. This chapter introduces a novel framework that shows how the academic and operational competencies lead to the life-world becoming of students and contributes to the existing university ecosystems theory. Based on the explored literature and the authors' long-term experience in higher education, this chapter also outlines the implications for educational researchers, practical implications for educational practitioners, and broader society.

title: A Computational Study of Derivative Pricing under Stochastic Volatility Using the Black–Scholes Framework

detail.title: A Computational Study of Derivative Pricing under Stochastic Volatility Using the Black–Scholes Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: This working paper presents a computational study of derivative pricing using the Black–Scholes framework, evaluated against real S&P 500 (SPX) option market data. By implementing a full pricing pipeline including Greeks and implied volatility extraction, the study exposes systematic pricing deviations across strikes, consistent with volatility smile phenomena. These mispricings highlight the limitations of constant-volatility assumptions and motivate the need for richer stochastic volatility models. The paper concludes with open research directions involving the Heston model and calibration challenges. This work forms the basis of a broader research agenda in mathematical finance, combining computational experimentation with theoretical development.

title: The Paris Climate Agreement as Benchmark for Buildings and Companies

detail.title: The Paris Climate Agreement as Benchmark for Buildings and Companies
detail.abstract:
Piazolo, Daniel, „The Paris Climate Agreement as Benchmark for Buildings and Companies“, IOP Conference Series; Earth and Environment Science, 2022, Vol. 1078.
The real estate market has a high obligation, but also many opportunities, to tackle climate change. The real estate sector is responsible for 40% of energy consumption and 36% of CO2 emissions in the EU. The global temperature must not rise by more than 1.5° Celsius compared to pre-industrial times in order to avert serious consequences of climate change. 195 countries agreed on this target by signing the Paris Climate Agreement in 2015 and thus also set the legislative framework and the desired direction of development for societies, companies and buildings. 
The Paris Climate Agreement can be used to establish a benchmark by showing which development routes are necessary to be compliant with the Agreement. It can be examined which adjustments are necessary to limit maximum global warming to 1.5° Celsius. By matching specific properties against such a benchmark, it can be worked out which properties are at risk of no longer being usable/rentable because they cannot meet the expected increases in environmental regulations, CO2 pricing, building standards and market expectations. This can be used to address transitory climate change risks.

title: From incentives to adoption: A decadal review of India's EV subsidy effectiveness
affiliations: University of Oxford - Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, Independent and Independent

detail.title: From incentives to adoption: A decadal review of India's EV subsidy effectiveness
detail.abstract: India has used a wide range of central and state subsidies to accelerate electric vehicle (EV) adoption over the past decade, but the effectiveness of this support across segments remains unclear. This paper assembles a 10-year (2014–2023) state-level panel of EV sales, policy variables and cost indicators to evaluate how demand- and supply-side incentives have shaped uptake in five major vehicle categories. Using difference-in-differences and synthetic control methods, we find that higher purchase subsidies under FAME-II, reinforced by supportive state policies, substantially increased electric two-wheeler sales, yet EVs still account for only a small share of total two-wheeler registrations. Early, relatively modest subsidies for passenger three-wheelers appear to have helped this segment reach a self-sustaining phase, where commercial fundamentals now dominate. Cargo three-wheelers and commercial four-wheelers respond strongly to improvements in operating cost economics and targeted state incentives, while generous e-bus subsidies have translated into only limited adoption because of procurement design and financing constraints. Across segments, we estimate sizeable “market multiplier” effects, with each rupee of public support leveraging several rupees of total market value. The results highlight the importance of segment-specific policy design, clearer long-term subsidy trajectories and complementary non-price interventions for India’s next generation of EV schemes, including PM E-DRIVE.

title: To Tariff or Not to Tariff? That is the Question (before the U.S. Supreme Court)
affiliations: Texas A&M University (TAMU), School of Law and Texas A&M University (TAMU), School of Law

detail.title: To Tariff or Not to Tariff? That is the Question (before the U.S. Supreme Court)
detail.abstract: This working paper summarises and analyses the legal question before the U.S. Supreme Court in the case of Learning Res., Inc. v. Trump. The issue is whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), 50 U.S.C. § 1701 et seq., authorises the President to impose import duties as part of a national-emergency regime aimed at correcting large and persistent U.S. trade deficits. Because Article I vests Congress with the power to lay and collect taxes, duties and imposts, and the Court has signalled heightened scrutiny under the non-delegation and major-questions doctrines, commentators expect the Court to reject this assertion of executive tariff authority. However, this note identifies prior appellate and Supreme Court decisions under the Trading with the Enemy Act (TWEA), which employed similar language, upholding regulatory tariffs as a valid delegation for national security. It suggests that a narrow regulatory-tariff exception could emerge or that the Court may remand for fact-finding, leaving room for limited emergency tariffs.

title: Social Engineering Through Schools
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of California, Berkeley and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Social Engineering Through Schools
detail.abstract: We study how schools embed themselves in communities and, in doing so, function as instruments of social engineering that influence political and cultural change. Our focus is on schools run by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organization. We compile new data on the establishment years and locations of these schools and link it to constituency-level electoral outcomes for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), India’s dominant right-wing party. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we  find that the presence of RSS schools leads to a persistent rise in BJP vote share and a higher probability of BJP victories in subsequent elections. These schools also lead to cultural change. Vegetarianism rises in nearby villages, especially among upper-caste households, the traditional supporters of the BJP. The share of children given Hindu deity names, particularly those of the Vaishnavite pantheon, increases in affected areas after the setting up of schools. Together, these patterns point to a process of gradual identity activation through sustained community engagement. To examine the mechanisms in greater detail, we survey a random subsample of schools—both RSS-run and non-RSS, non-government institutions—across four districts in Bihar. The survey results indicate that, relative to close-by non-RSS private schools, RSS schools are substantially more likely to engage in Hindu religious programming  as well as community engagement that involves not only students but also parents and local communities.

title: Facility Management Outsourcing: Innovation in Contract Models

detail.abstract: Case Objectives and Usage This case is developed for degree in property and facility management (PFM), particularly in courses covering contract governance, outsourcing performance, change and conflict management. The target student groups are MBA, EMBA, and graduate students in facility management (FM). Through this case study, students can understand various forms of business outsourcing, implementation criteria, and subcontract arrangements. The case focuses on making decision on a new contract model, resolving dilemma between business and functional departments, and selecting an appropriate business partner. The case allows students to understand complexity in contract governance and conflicting interests in a realworld setting.

detail.abstract: Sustainability and return on stock represent crucial factors in a company's development. Board gender diversity and financial performance can influence a company's Sustainability and return on stock. This study employs a quantitative research method analyzing data from 17 companies, utilizing financial reports from 2018 to 2021. The research findings indicate no significant influence of board gender diversity and financial performance on stock return through a company's Sustainability. These findings underscore the complexity of the dynamics between these factors, emphasizing the need for an integrated approach in corporate management to achieve an optimal balance between Sustainability, return on stock, and inclusive business practices.

title: Why Academia Is Stupid: Exposing Compensatory Nurturance Syndrome and the Gordon Ramsay Ego Boomerang™

detail.title: Why Academia Is Stupid: Exposing Compensatory Nurturance Syndrome and the Gordon Ramsay Ego Boomerang™
detail.abstract:
This working paper introduces a unified psychological framework integrating Compensatory Nurturance Syndrome (CNS), a newly identified set of ego-defensive distortions (the Gordon Ramsay Ego Boomerang™ effects), and Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) emotional-regulation principles. Existing academic models explain attachment, trauma, ego defense, conflict, and addiction separately; this work demonstrates how their interaction produces predictable interpersonal dysfunction and systemic failures across domestic violence, addiction treatment, communication breakdowns, and social institutions.

Using a conceptual synthesis of attachment theory, interpersonal neurobiology, attribution bias research, and DBT’s fact-checking and radical-acceptance skills, this paper maps how maladaptive nurturance styles create lifelong emotional vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities activate eleven micro-defensive distortions—Mirrorback, Projection Shield, Inversion Defense, Moral Superiorization, Ostrich Loop, and others—that escalate conflict, distort feedback, and undermine accountability.

This model argues that psychology is not incorrect, but incomplete; the missing integration point is the interaction of nurturance origin + ego-defense cascade + emotional-regulation failure. By naming these mechanisms and demonstrating their relevance to DV/IPV misdiagnosis, addiction relapse, conflict cycles, and emotional-intelligence deficits, this paper offers a new foundation for clinical practice, relationship education, accountability training, and institutional reform.

title: Alcohol Prohibition and Attitudes towards Spousal Violence against Women
affiliations: Le Moyne College and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Alcohol Prohibition and Attitudes towards Spousal Violence against Women

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We study the effects of a comprehensive, statewide alcohol ban on attitudes towards spousal violence in the Indian state of Bihar. Using a triple-difference framework, we document significant improvements in attitudes towards spousal violence involving scenarios reflecting an increase in women’s personal freedom, such as going out without telling the husband and arguing with the husband. We observe no change in attitudes involving a wife’s supposedly traditional responsibilities, such as looking after kids, cooking, and having sex with the husband. We argue and provide evidence that alcohol consumption exerts a significant income effect, souring spousal relations that causes men’s attitudes towards wife-beating to worsen. Our findings suggest that the alcohol ban benefited women of weaker sections (SC/ST communities) of society the most. We conclude that while such policies can empower women in certain walks of life, they are insufficient to alter long-rooted patriarchal beliefs.

title: Enhancing Medical Image Analysis with Advanced CNN Architectures: Contrast Optimization, Explainability, and Lightweight Models
affiliations: Chandigarh University, Chandigarh University, Chandigarh University and

detail.title: Enhancing Medical Image Analysis with Advanced CNN Architectures: Contrast Optimization, Explainability, and Lightweight Models

detail.abstract: The application of neural networks has demonstrated enormous promise in improving diagnostic efficiency and accuracy in the rapidly changing field of medical diagnostics. This study explores the convergence of neural networks in medical diagnosis systems, emphasizing the capacity of these networks to handle large, multi-dimensional data sets for accurate and timely diagnosis of a range of medical disorders. These systems use sophisticated neural architectures to speed up decision-making, lower human error, and enhance patient outcomes. In order to provide insights into the future of AI-driven healthcare solutions, the study delves deeper into the effects of deep learning approaches, model training convergence, and their application across many medical domains. Through a comprehensive analysis of neural network convergence, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing development of intelligent diagnostic systems that will reshape modern healthcare delivery.

title: Cheaper and Better? Explaining a Newborn Mortality Advantage at Public Versus Private Hospitals in India
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Cheaper and Better? Explaining a Newborn Mortality Advantage at Public Versus Private Hospitals in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper is a dissertation chapter and has received no direct funding apart from a summer writing grant from the UT-Austin College of Liberal Arts.

detail.abstract: Public provision of healthcare may reduce efficiency but can also correct market failures. I study two large Indian states where high mortality rates make effects detectable and weak regulation allows provider incentives to operate without constraint. In these states, public (government-run) clinics and hospitals charge less for care and have poorer patients than private clinics and hospitals-yet, puzzlingly, births there survive at much higher rates. I show that these public facilities reduce the rate of newborn death by over 25 per thousand births, over half the rate of death for private-facility births. I use two complementary empirical strategies. First, to address selection, I estimate the slope of village neonatal mortality with respect to the public-private birth share; if facility type didn't matter, and the observed differences were entirely due to selection, then this slope would be zero. Second, I estimate the spatial discontinuity in mortality at district borders, which exogenously shift public use for otherwise-similar nearby births. I present evidence that the mortality gap operates through interventions that follow separation of mothers and babies, a pattern consistent with pay-per-service incentives that reward additional procedures in private facilities. These results suggest that if private providers treated patients identically to public providers, they would prevent over 37,000 children's deaths each year.

detail.abstract: This article explores the intersection of marketing and management within the contemporary field of journalism. As digital transformation reshapes the media landscape, traditional journalistic practices are being integrated with market-oriented strategies and managerial innovation. The paper examines how media organizations can adapt to shifting audience behavior, economic pressures, and technological disruption through the application of strategic marketing, branding, audience analytics, and organizational leadership. Drawing on both theoretical frameworks and current industry practices, the study offers a comprehensive view of how journalism can maintain its public mission while achieving economic sustainability and operational efficiency.

title: Credit Rating as A Determinant of FDI Flows in Egypt

detail.title: Credit Rating as A Determinant of FDI Flows in Egypt
detail.abstract:

detail.abstract: The increasing frequency of extreme weather events poses significant socioeconomic challenges, particularly for vulnerable populations in developing countries. This paper investigates the impact of temperature exposure on intimate partner violence (IPV) using individual-level data from the 2008 Bolivian Demographic and Health Survey matched with high-resolution daily climate data. Employing a temperature binning approach with fixed effects, I find substantial heterogeneous effects by altitude: in low-altitude areas, ten additional days of extreme cold (below 21°C) or extreme heat (33°C or higher) significantly increase IPV incidence by 3.6 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively, while moderate cold temperatures reduce IPV incidence. Moreover, cold exposure increases IPV through heightened male alcohol consumption and income instability, particularly in rural and indigenous communities, while heat exposure reduces women's employment in urban, non-indigenous households. Overall, the results demonstrate that the effects of temperature exposure are highly contextual and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for climate adaptation policies that are sensitive to socioeconomic status and gender so that they can contribute to the broader goal of reducing violence against women.

detail.abstract:
The liberal welfare state is a design failure, structurally insolvent due to its continuous externalization of long-term, unpriced costs (Generational Debt, Infrastructure Decay, Social Atomization) onto future generations. This paper introduces Structural Neo-Pragmatism, a non-ideological governing platform that replaces the current model with a system founded on the mathematically verifiable principle: The long-term Structural Cost of Stability is always fiscally superior to the recurring cost of chaos.

Solvency is enforced through two core mechanisms:

The Commitment Contract: Policy is executed via voluntary exchanges where citizens and businesses receive an Irresistible Incentive (e.g., tax-free, high-yield retirement via the GRA) in exchange for a Structural Commitment to collective solvency (e.g., national debt amortization).

Quantified Solvency (SUR/TSUR): Every policy is mandated to prove its net fiscal superiority via the Structural Utility Ratio (SUR > 1.0). The overall platform is proven resilient with a Total Structural Utility Ratio (TSUR) of 1.14 at a conservative baseline, leveraging high-yield pillars (like the Democratic Integrity Covenant - DIC) to structurally support necessities (like the National Skill Covenant - NSC).

This blueprint provides a complete, quantifiable, and resilient architectural defense against the existential costs of collapse, shifting governance from short-term political preference to an enforced, long-term actuarial mandate overseen by the National Structural Solvency Authority (NSSA).

title: Carbon Labels and Consumer Flight Choices
affiliations: and New York University - Stern School of Business

detail.title: Carbon Labels and Consumer Flight Choices
detail.abstract: Climate change concerns have led many companies to adopt labels that disclose their carbon footprint to consumers. However, the effectiveness of such labels for both firm outcomes and consumer behavior remains largely unexplored. To measure these effects, we rely on data from a major flight search platform that exogenously timed the introduction of carbon labels for qualifying flights on its platform. These data allow us to use quasi-experimental methods to understand how labels affect firms and consumers. We find that consumers are more likely to make a purchase when labels are present, which benefits the platform. However, such converting consumers are not necessarily more likely to buy a lower-emission/labeled flight. In addition, they search more when environmental information is available. Finally, among a subset of similar flights, we find that options with a label have higher conversion rates. Our findings suggest consumers value/trust the platform more when labels are present, but will only switch to labeled options if they can avoid sacrificing other product features. Heterogeneity across traveler types and political orientation is also explored. These results highlight nuanced effects of carbon labeling, offering insights for firms and policymakers designing sustainability disclosures in digital marketplaces.

detail.abstract: We investigate the implications of heterogeneous employer learning on education signaling and workers sorting across industries. In the equilibrium of our model, higher-ability workers join industries with faster employer learning speeds, resulting in a matching distortion of workers and industries. In addition, our results are robust to varying degrees of asymmetric employer learning, and establish that industry choice itself serves as a signal of worker ability. Finally, our theoretical approach suggests a novel perspective on a heretofore neglected labor market puzzle, i.e., why few of the richest individuals have obtained higher degrees of education.

detail.abstract: Rust Belt cities like Pittsburgh have played a pivotal role in recent presidential elections, emerging as a bellwether of national political shifts. In Southwestern Pennsylvania, decades of deindustrialization have left deep economic and social scars, fueling a sense of abandonment in many working-class communities. These conditions have sharpened partisan and racial divides, as some neighborhoods trend toward conservative populism while others remain deeply progressive. This brief examines how polarization, shaped by economic decline, racial segregation, and shifting political identities, affects local governance and social cohesion across Pittsburgh and its surrounding towns.

detail.title: Double Peer Effects, Deregulation, and Audit Fees: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper examines client and auditor peer effects on audit pricing and the impact of the deregulation of audit pricing in 2014 on the double peer effects in China. We provide the first empirical evidence that both clients and auditors imitate peer audit fees, and these peer effects are stronger in high information asymmetry settings, partly reflecting irrational herding rather than rational learning. However, increased competition resulting from the deregulation significantly reduces auditors' peer effects (especially among Big 4 auditors that pursue differentiation strategies) and this reduction is associated with audit quality improvement. This study deepens understanding of peer effects in audit pricing and offers valuable insights for policymakers and regulators in promoting market-oriented competition and enhancing audit quality.

detail.abstract: Universal Basic Income (UBI) presents a potential solution to numerous socioeconomic challenges. However, its implementation remains constrained by funding issues. detail.abstract: Low worker substitutability is a labor market friction that makes worker turnover costly to the firm. By bridging the literature on worker substitutability with the literature on labor supply effects of retirement reforms, I show that the older workers who posses specific skills and who are more difficult to substitutable internally by coworkers and externally by new hires or by automation are more likely to increase their employment in response to the reform that resulted in an increase of retirement age. To address endogeneity in labor supply decisions at an older age, I use regression discontinuity design by utilizing a reform in Germany that scrapped the opportunities to retire before the age 63. My results show that workers’ labor supply response to the retirement reform is not solely made at the individual level, but is coordinated with firms dependent on their ease of substitutability, thus mitigating the costly turnover for firms. When analyzing the spillovers on coworkers and firms, I find that there are negative effects on hiring and promotions, especially of middle-aged women. The longer planning horizon specific to this reform does not eliminate the adjustment costs for establishments because of the frictions associated with worker turnover.
