detail.abstract:
Purpose : Increasing research on multi-channel identifies various disconnected factors influencing customer decisionmaking
behavior. Collecting and synthesizing this data was imperative to provide practitioners with pertinent insights. This
paper examined the current research on multi-channel retailing consumer decision outcomes (CDOs) from the lens of
consumer perceived value (CPV).
Methodology : This study employed a systematic literature review to delineate the existing knowledge at the junction of CPV
and CDO in multi-channel (siloed or integrated) retailing.
Findings : A systematic review of 152 peer-reviewed articles published in English-language journals indicated that
multi-channel CDOs are predominantly examined as a consequence of the perceived value of multi-channel dimensions rather than linked to retailing marketing and management. This study introduced a conceptual framework for multi-channel CDOs’ antecedents, episodes, and consequences.
Practical Implications : The results indicated techniques for utilizing customer decision outcomes to enhance returns for retail marketers and managers. These insights will assist field personnel in attaining consumer decision-making behavior
objectives.
Originality : This is among the first studies to conduct a systematic review of exhaustive peer-reviewed articles to delineate
existing gaps and potential for future research by mapping the intersection of multi-channel customer-perceived value and
CDOs. Further, this study provided various findings on retailing studies by segregating findings between articles
corresponding to multichannel and omnichannel.

title: Impulse Buying in the Digital Age: A Conceptual Review and Research Agenda Toward an Integrated Theory of Spontaneous Consumption
affiliations: and NIT Trichy

detail.title: Impulse Buying in the Digital Age: A Conceptual Review and Research Agenda Toward an Integrated Theory of Spontaneous Consumption
detail.abstract: Twelve years after our foundational synthesis (Muruganantham & Bhakat, 2013), impulse buying research stands at a theoretical crossroads. While the field has proliferated and generated close to 1,000 citations and hundreds of empirical studies , fundamental questions about the nature of impulsivity in consumption remain unresolved. This conceptual review argues that impulse buying scholarship has become ‘empirically rich but theoretically stagnant’, recycling established frameworks without advancing our understanding of why consumers act spontaneously. Drawing on a chronological narrative analysis of landmark studies from 2013-2025, this paper identifies three theoretical transitions: (1) From trait-based to context-dependent impulsivity (challenging the assumption that some consumers are inherently impulsive); (2) From affective disruption to motivated spontaneity (reframing impulse as purposeful rather than irrational); and (3) From individual psychology to algorithmic orchestration (recognizing that digital environments systematically engineer spontaneous behavior). Through critical engagement with cutting-edge research in neuroscience, behavioral economics, and platform capitalism, I propose an ‘Integrated Theory of Spontaneous Consumption’ that reconceptualizes impulse buying not as a breakdown in self-control, but as an adaptive response to information-rich, time-constrained decision environments. This framework bridges micro-level psychological mechanisms with macro-level technological architectures, offering testable propositions about when, why, and how consumers engage in spontaneous purchasing. The review concludes with a transformative research agenda emphasizing: neurobiological substrates of spontaneous choice, ethical implications of algorithmic nudging, cross-cultural manifestations of spontaneity, and the sustainability paradox of impulsive consumption. By elevating impulse buying from a managerial concern to a window into fundamental questions about human agency, this synthesis aims to reinvigorate theoretical inquiry in our field.

It can stimulate local economies by offering jobs, supporting local suppliers, and promoting cultural exchange. Moreover, it can promote sustainable practices such as preserving cultural heritage, reducing environmental impacts, and enhancing community involvement. The significance of tourism entrepreneurship lies in identifying opportunities, leveraging resources, and implementing creative ideas to serve tourists while generating economic gain. However, the tourism industry is highly competitive, seasonal, sensitive to external shocks, and based on intangible experience making it challenging for tourism entrepreneurs. Traditional tourism industries are being reshaped by technological advancement, offering new business models to entrepreneurs. Despite developments, there is a lack of comprehensive frameworks that integrate unique characteristics of tourism with entrepreneurial theories. The paper contributes by providing a conceptual framework for introduction to tourism entrepreneurship, highlighting its significance, opportunities, and challenges and exploring factors contributing to entrepreneurial success in tourism. detail.abstract: This project introduces Card Generator, a tool built for real-world use that automatically creates logos and cards. The system uses a React (Vite) website, a Node.js service that works with Gemini to improve prompts, and a Python FastAPI service that sends image requests to various AI backends like Hugging Face, Stability.ai, or a local diffusion setup [3], [5], [18]. detail.abstract: The pervasive influence of digitalization mandates corporate engagement on social media platforms due to continuous user growth. This investigation empirically assesses the influence of social media utilization on the core attributes of luxury brands: exclusivity and brand image. Luxury brands are fundamentally characterized by these attributes (among six key facets) and traditionally leverage channels like print, out-of-home marketing, and word-of-mouth. Nevertheless, social media offers advanced strategies, including influencer marketing, paid advertisements, and user-generated content, which facilitate rapid, broad audience reach and provide targeted control options. The critical necessity for luxury brands is identifying appropriate social media strategies. To rigorously analyze consumer perceptions, a choice experiment methodology was employed. Empirical results indicated that specific factors influence both exclusivity and brand image, although many variables exhibit no relationship with these constructs. Consequently, the effects and resulting influences are highly individualized, compelling luxury brands to autonomously determine the most effective digital strategies that uphold their defining characteristics.

title: Self- or Rival-Revelation? Dynamic Information Design in Sequential Competition
affiliations: University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois, Yale University, Department of Economics and Tianjin University

detail.title: Self- or Rival-Revelation? Dynamic Information Design in Sequential Competition
detail.abstract:
In uncertain environments, consumers seek and interpret information to reduce ambiguity and guide their choices and purchase decisions. In this paper, we study how firms strategically design information about either themselves or their rivals to influence consumer purchase decisions in dynamic competition. We construct a dynamic Bayesian persuasion model in which a leader firm and a follower firm sequentially design and send their information to consumers to strategically shape consumers’ beliefs on the two firms’ product match. Our analysis shows that, strikingly, the leader firm may choose to “serve” the competing rival firm with a high risk gambler strategy of fully providing the rival information to consumers, especially
when consumers have moderate prior beliefs for the leader firm. In addition, when consumers have relatively high prior beliefs for the leader firm, the leader firm may surprisingly choose a downward twisted self-revelation strategy, intentionally disseminating unfavorable signals about itself despite favorable product match to manipulate consumer purchase. Finally, we show that an increase in competition may intensify information manipulation.

title: Limiting Accessibility: How Targeting Consumers with Disabilities Constrains Acceptable Prices for Innovations
affiliations: Tilburg University, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) and Erasmus University - Rotterdam School of Management

detail.title: Limiting Accessibility: How Targeting Consumers with Disabilities Constrains Acceptable Prices for Innovations
detail.abstract: People with disabilities constitute 15% of the world’s population and hold a buying power of $1.9 trillion. However, few companies offer products tailored to the needs of this segment, making it important to understand how mass-market consumers react to innovations that target people with disabilities. Nine studies and six supplementary studies (total N = 11,237) reveal that innovations that target consumers with disabilities are subjected to comparatively stronger scrutiny by mass-market consumers. Specifically, consumers find charging price premiums for innovative products less acceptable when they are targeted at people with disabilities. The aversion to targeting this segment only occurs in the presence of a price premium and persists even when firms provide cost justifications for the relatively higher prices. Drawing on research on disability stereotypes, we isolate pity for people with disabilities as a critical driver of these reactions. Variations in pity across disabilities are related to the acceptability of a price premium for adaptive innovations. These findings are suggestive of a novel form of paternalism against consumers with disabilities. Paradoxically, this view may render the marketplace less inclusive for consumers with disabilities, as it could penalize companies that provide more options for this underserved segment.

title: Is Channel Conflict Bad for Business? A Competency-Based Theory and Empirical Evidence
affiliations: Laurentian University, University of Guelph, Gordon S. Lang School of Business and Economics and University of Graz

detail.title: Is Channel Conflict Bad for Business? A Competency-Based Theory and Empirical Evidence

keywords: Networks L22 -Firm Organization and Market Structure M21 -Business Economics C23 -Panel Data Models

detail.abstract: The impact of conflict between marketing channel partners is often traced to the transaction costs of dealing with the feuds and linked negatively to business performance. However, is such channel conflict really bad for business? We contend that it is not so and that conflict's net impact on business performance is nuanced. Channel conflicts are opportunities to learn which trigger myriad bilateral remedial adaptations, benefiting the partnerships. This tension between the deadweight loss of transaction costs and the advantage of learning means that the net impact of conflict will depend on the firms' competencies to benefit from learning and to keep the transaction costs from escalating. We incorporate these in our theory and test the propositions using data from a panel of 513 franchise firms over six years (2010-2015). Our data comprises information on litigation, franchise contract terms, and revenue extracted from Franchise Disclosure Documents (FDD), Entrepreneur Magazine, and Franchise Times rankings. We find that the negative impact of conflict is only true above a threshold level of conflict. At lower levels, conflict is associated with improved business performance-thus, an inverted U-shaped conflict-performance relationship. Consistent with the propositions, firm competencies reflected in the age and size of the firm, moderate the conflict-performance curve, shifting the apex to the right and flattening/steepening the slopes predictably. Our results are robust to different model specifications, measures of performance, and endogeneity considerations. For managers, the results indicate how certain competencies are critical to designing resilient marketing channels.

title: Choice Set Size Neglect in Predicting Others' Preferences
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Georgetown University and Vanderbilt University - Owen Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Choice Set Size Neglect in Predicting Others' Preferences
detail.abstract: An inherent feature of any choice is the set size from which that choice is made-i.e., the number of available options in a choice set. Choice set size impacts the likelihood of landing on a more-preferred option: Larger sets are more likely to contain an option matching one's preferences. Despite this, six preregistered experiments (N = 10,092 U.S. adults) demonstrate that people consistently underestimate the effect of set size when predicting others' liking for a chosen option. We propose this effect arises because, although people recognize that set size predicts liking of a chosen option, they typically fail to attend to it when considering others' choices. As such, this effect attenuates when attention is drawn to set size, specifically: (a) when considering multiple set sizes simultaneously, (b) when the decision process is framed as ranking rather than choosing, or (c) when prompted to recall set size before predicting others' preferences.

title: Climate Models: The Politics of Their Consumption Patterns

detail.title: Climate Models: The Politics of Their Consumption Patterns
detail.abstract: This study reconceptualizes climate models as cultural and political objects of consumption rather than as neutral scientific forecasts. It argues that the uptake or rejection of climate models is mediated less by their technical validity than by the cultural logics through which individuals interpret them and the media frames that amplify these logics. Drawing on the cultural theory of risk and semiotic perspectives on meaning-making, the analysis segments responses into four orientations: fatalists, who disengage under apocalyptic framings; hierarchists, who resonate with institutional authority and ordered responses; individualists, who resist models perceived as threatening economic freedom or personal autonomy; and egalitarians, who embrace justice-oriented narratives that mandate collective transformation. These categories function as heuristic tools, recognizing that real-world responses are often hybrid and contextdependent. Media coverage plays a pivotal role in sustaining these patterned tendencies, transforming scientific models into contested cultural texts. By situating climate models within consumer culture, the study demonstrates how a cultural consumption lens can inform climate communication, offering pathways for more inclusive, audience-sensitive messaging that bridges ideological divides while advancing coordinated climate action.

title: The Impact of Financing on Multisided Platforms: Evidence from the Digital Asset Market
affiliations: , Indian School of Business and Yale School of Management

detail.title: The Impact of Financing on Multisided Platforms: Evidence from the Digital Asset Market
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of introducing financing on the market outcomes of a multisided digital asset platform, and examine whether platforms can use financing as a growth lever. The platform intermediates buyers and sellers of digital assets, specifically Non-Fungible Tokens (or NFTs). The focal platform, Blur, introduced financing (Buy-Now-Pay-Later) for some product collections, holding the digital asset as collateral. The loans are provided by other users. Using a unique dataset from both the focal platform and its biggest competitor, we identify the impact of financing on buyers' purchases and sellers' listing decisions. We find that offering financing increases quantities sold and total revenue for treated collections, without affecting selling prices. Moreover, financing does not influence the sales and revenues at the rival platform. Decomposing these effects, we find that supply-side responses account for only 26% of the increase in sales. On the demand side, existing users exhibit a "flight to quality," purchasing higher-quality products when financing is available. While financing attracts new users from rival platforms to act as lenders on Blur, these users do not shift their trading activity to Blur. Consequently, financing does not expand Blur's overall user base, and its spillover effects on the competing platform remain minimal.

title: Do Accessibility Features Improve the Outdoor Mobility of People with Disabilities? An Empirical Study on Amap
affiliations: Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, School of Management, Jinan University,  and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Do Accessibility Features Improve the Outdoor Mobility of People with Disabilities? An Empirical Study on Amap
detail.abstract: As of 2023, an estimated 1.3 billion people, or roughly 16% of the global population, have a disability. Big tech companies have played a significant role in improving disability inclusion by using technology to increase accessibility of their products/services. Although these approaches are promising, empirical evidence on their actual impact remains scarce. In this study, we examine how the accessibility feature in a location-based service app affects the outdoor mobility of disabled users. Using individual-level data from Amap, we find that this feature significantly increases disabled users’ exploration of outdoor spaces, whether through search or walk navigation. The effect holds for nearly all subgroups studied and either reduces or enlarges the gap among them. In addition, users alter their behavior after adoption by searching for more distant locations but walking to closer destinations than before.

title: Predicting Brand Loyalty to Manufacturer-Sponsored Brands in an Omnichannel Environment : A Configurational Perspective

detail.title: Predicting Brand Loyalty to Manufacturer-Sponsored Brands in an Omnichannel Environment : A Configurational Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors certify that they have no affiliations with or involvement in any organization or entity with any financial or non-financial interest in the subject matter or materials discussed in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Purpose : Drawing upon the configuration perspective, this study examined how combinations of different omnichannel capability dimensions from the supply side lead to brand loyalty for manufacturer-sponsored brands. Omnichannel integration is a long-drawn process that integrates a variety of dimensions. This induced us to understand how various combinations of dimensions lead to loyalty. Design : The study used a multi-level design based on the data collected on 43 manufacturer-sponsor brands from experts and 2,320 consumers through a structured questionnaire. Using the Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) method, the study explored the different pathways through which seven omnichannel dimensions, namely siloed retail mix, integrated marketing communication, integrated consumer order fulfillment, and information access, continuity of foundationals, rearend system consolidation, and organization transfiguration, lead to demand-side brand loyalty. Findings : The results showed that these seven omnichannel dimensions are sufficient conditions for achieving brand loyalty. The truth table analysis showed seven pathways for omnichannel integration efforts to improve brand loyalty. Practical Implications : The study presented seven combinations of internal resource-based omnichannel capability dimensions for practical application, which may be implemented to attain loyalty objectives. Originality : This is among the first studies to consider a comprehensive combination of omnichannel integration dimensions and their effects on brand loyalty, unlike previous studies that focused on such limited dimensions. This is also the first study to consider omnichannel integration of manufacturer brands, while previous studies have focused on multi-brand retailers. Further, through a configurational perspective, the study allays the methodological limitations of the variance-based approaches in the previous studies.

title: The Labor Market Consequences of Mass College Expansion: Evidence from China

detail.title: The Labor Market Consequences of Mass College Expansion: Evidence from China

declarations.funderStatement: No external funding from any commercial, non-profit, or government agency was received for this research.

detail.abstract: From 1999 to 2020 China undertook one of the world's largest expansions of higher education, increasing full-time enrollment from 4 to 32 million. This paper provides new evidence on how this reform reshaped wages and employment at both the worker and labor market levels. Using newly assembled data from policy documents, I exploit the staggered openings of new colleges and universities across cities for causal identification. The new higher education institutions significantly increased enrollment and trained more than 118,000 new graduates per city within a decade. About 45% of the graduate supply was absorbed locally into high-skill services, manufacturing, and state-owned sectors. Yet, these expanding cities also experienced rising unemployment and slower wage growth. Worker-level evidence reveals a large negative wage effect concentrated among young graduates: the college premium fell sharply for post-reform cohorts but remained stable for earlier cohorts. Using a structural labor supply-demand framework, I estimate a very low degree of substitutability across college cohorts, and show that it originates from the declining average quality of recent graduates. The reform created a substantial cohort-specific supply shock that outpaced demand growth, leading to an emerging wage gap between younger and older workers.

title: Evaluation of ingredient list, food additives and claims on plant-based industrialized products and analysis of purchase motivation by Brazilian consumers
affiliations: Universidade Federal de Uberlandia, Universidade Federal de Uberlandia, Universidade Federal de Uberlandia, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidade Federal de Uberlandia, Universidade Federal de Uberlandia and Universidade Federal de Uberlandia

detail.title: Evaluation of ingredient list, food additives and claims on plant-based industrialized products and analysis of purchase motivation by Brazilian consumers
detail.abstract: The market for plant-based industrialized products has been growing in Brazil and the lack of specific regulations for these products has raised concerns regarding the clarity of the information presented on their labels. The objective was to evaluate the ingredient lists, food additives and claims on plant-based industrialized products and to analyze the purchase motivations of Brazilian consumers. This is a cross-sectional descriptive study, in which 198 labels and the purchasing motivations of 232 consumers were analyzed. The results showed that 105 (53%) products featured nutritional claims, and 171 (86.4%) presented positive claims (not covered by current legislation). Among the 232 consumers, 31.5% believed that plant-based industrialized products were more nutritious and 59.3% of the positive claims were related to "nutrients, ingredients, composition, physiological effects and health." The nutritional claim "lactose-free" appeared on 44 (28.2%) products, making it the most frequent. In conclusion, the use of nutritional and positive claims on plant-based industrialized products requires caution, as it may influence consumers' food choices and lead to misconceptions about their healthfulness. This study highlights the urgent need for Brazilian regulations concerning plant-based industrialized products in order to mitigate quality misrepresentations and promote transparency for consumers. It may also serve as a foundation for the development and implementation of a technical identity and quality regulation for plant-based industrialized products in the Brazilian market.

title: Buy Now, Play Never: Why Consumers Purchase Things They Don't Use
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School and Tongji University - School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Buy Now, Play Never: Why Consumers Purchase Things They Don't Use
detail.abstract: In this paper, we study non-usage, where consumers purchase products that they never use. This behavior may lower consumer welfare and can inflate demand. Using an Empirics-First approach (Golder et al., 2023), we assemble and analyze a rich panel data set from Steam, the leading digital PC gaming platform, linking purchases to subsequent usage over an eight-year horizon for tens of thousands of users. We estimate that 36.8 percent of purchased games are never played, representing 28.9 percent of platform revenue and approximately $849 million in 2017 spending. Combining model-free evidence with descriptive regressions, we document empirical patterns in non-usage and assess which mechanisms align with them. The evidence is most consistent with behavioral mechanisms, particularly inattention and overestimation of variety seeking, suggesting that non-usage largely reflects consumer mistakes rather than utility-maximizing behavior. We then test whether unused purchases reduce future engagement and find no decline in subsequent purchases or playtime. Non-usage raises short-run revenue without eroding longer-run platform activity. We conclude with recommendations for how consumers, platforms, and regulators can manage non-usage.

title: Protected Heterogeneity: A Variance-Based Framework for Fair Algorithmic Personalization
affiliations: , Harvard Business School and Harvard Business School - Marketing Unit

detail.title: Protected Heterogeneity: A Variance-Based Framework for Fair Algorithmic Personalization
detail.abstract: Effective personalization requires heterogeneity-the differences between users in their characteristics, preferences, behaviors, and contexts-that makes differential treatment valuable. Some of this heterogeneity, however, may stem from legally or ethically protected attributes such as race, gender, or age. We introduce protected heterogeneity as the share of variation in an algorithmically produced score explained by protected attributes and their proxies. We derive a corresponding diagnostic measure, R^2_prot, which is bounded, interpretable, and does not depend on arbitrary decision thresholds. This model-agnostic diagnostic tool can be used to identify and quantify fairness concerns by measuring the extent to which protected attributes influence algorithmic predictions. It is a variance-based, pre-decision measure of fairness that can be used to audit both existing systems and new algorithms prior to deployment. In addition, by formalizing the estimation of R^2_prot, we introduce a straightforward method for removing protected heterogeneity through the construction of residualized scores. These residualized scores exhibit both individual-and group-level fairness guarantees, enabling decision makers to preserve the value of leveraging individual differences while ensuring that decisions are not systematically shaped by protected characteristics. Beyond a technical contribution, the diagnostic supports regulatory compliance, ethical objectives, and reputational risk management in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and employment.

title: Advertising as Information or Reminder: Efficiency Gains from Personalizing Ad Length and Frequency
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School, Pandora Media, Inc., Pandora Media, Inc. and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Advertising as Information or Reminder: Efficiency Gains from Personalizing Ad Length and Frequency
detail.abstract: We study the economics of advertising length using a large-scale randomized experiment on 18.3 million Pandora listeners. The experiment promoted a listening feature, randomly assigning listeners to advertising campaigns that varied in format (10 vs. 30 seconds) and frequency. Among listeners unfamiliar with the feature, both short and long ads produced incremental ad effects that persisted for up to two years, with the advantage of longer ads substantially larger. Among listeners already familiar, advertising effects dissipated within weeks, and the relative benefit of longer ads was much smaller. Using the randomized data, we conduct off-policy evaluation of counterfactual campaign designs and find that a personalized policy that optimally allocates ad length and frequency across users can increase incremental ad effects by about 30 percent. These results show that advertising plays different roles for different users, informing the unfamiliar and reminding the familiar, and that tailoring ad design to user characteristics can substantially improve campaign performance.

title: Digital transformation in emerging markets: Adoption dynamics of AI image generation in marketing practices
affiliations: American International University-Bangladesh

detail.title: Digital transformation in emerging markets: Adoption dynamics of AI image generation in marketing practices
detail.abstract: This study explores the key variables influencing the adoption of AI image generators in marketing in Bangladesh, emphasizing the mediated impact of perceived usefulness. The study examines the present extent of AI image generator use across marketing agencies in Bangladesh and offers suggestions for optimizing their application to enhance efficiency, creativity, and competitiveness. A quantitative research strategy was used, gathering primary data via a standardized questionnaire administered to 480 marketing experts. Following the screening process, 320 replies were considered valid. Convenience sampling was used, focusing on professionals engaged in choices about the implementation of AI image generators. The data was analyzed using Smart PLS, a statistical program for SEM, to investigate the connections between key components and behavioral intents. Research demonstrates that PE, EE, SI, FC, and ATT substantially affect the motivation to use AI image generators. Nonetheless, PR exerts no substantial influence. PU mediators the associations between PE, SI, and PR with BI, but it does not mediate EE, FC, or ATT. The research underscores the critical importance of perceived usefulness to boosting adoption. This study offers actionable insights for marketing companies, highlighting the need to augment perceived usefulness by showcasing the advantages of AI. It enhances the comprehension of AI adoption in developing areas, facilitating digital transformation. This research is novel in its contextual emphasis on Bangladesh and its use of perceived usefulness as a mediating variable.

title: How Group Reputation Threat Influences Reparatory Behavior
affiliations: ESADE - Ramon Llull University, FGV-EAESP, Ohio State University (OSU) and ESADE - Ramon Llull University

detail.title: How Group Reputation Threat Influences Reparatory Behavior

declarations.funderStatement: Sate Research Agency - reference number PID2020-117315GB-I00/AEI / 10.13039/501100011033 CAPES

detail.abstract: Consumers often act to correct the wrongdoings of people close to them, such as family members or friends. The current research demonstrates that consumers may also engage in a variety of reparatory behaviors-from a simple apology to gift-giving and tipping-to counter the misdeeds of ingroup strangers when their behavior threatens the reputation of their shared group identity. Across eight pre-registered experiments, the present research demonstrates that when an ingroup member commits a wrongdoing in the presence of outgroup observers, fellow ingroup members experience a threat to the group's reputation. This reputational threat evokes feelings of embarrassment and a motivation to distance the group identity from the transgressor, prompting reparatory behaviors such as apologizing, gift-giving, or tipping. These effects emerge across a range of social identities, including ethnicity, nationality, university affiliation, and sports team fandom. Importantly, this tendency is attenuated when other ingroup members have already taken action to restore the group's image. These findings reveal a powerful form of identity-driven consumer behavior, highlighting how concerns about group reputation can drive individuals to act, even for the misdeeds of ingroup strangers.

title: Off-Label Consumption and the Impact of Usage Frequency Cues on Potency Inferences
affiliations: Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University and University of Washington

detail.title: Off-Label Consumption and the Impact of Usage Frequency Cues on Potency Inferences
detail.abstract: This research investigates off-label use-instances where consumers deviate from marketed product guidelines by altering dosages, methods, or purposes. A descriptive pilot study documents the prevalence of this behavior in over-the-counter health and wellness categories. Across experiments, we demonstrate that usage frequency cues in marketing (e.g., "daily wellness" vs. "monthly use") systematically shape consumers' potency inferences and intentions to use products off-label. Holding product features constant, consumers perceive higherfrequency products as less potent and less susceptible to misuse-ironically increasing off-label use. These effects generalize across product categories (e.g., Ashwagandha, cannabis, melatonin) and user familiarity (e.g., cannabis users vs. non-users). Moderation evidence supports a potency account: explicit potency labeling mitigates the influence of frequency cues. Product purpose functions as a boundary condition-frequency cues guide off-label intentions when consumers consider repurposing therapeutic products for recreational use, but not the reverse. Overall, we introduce a novel psychological mechanism by which frequency cues shape potency inferences, thereby influencing downstream use decisions. These findings contribute to theories of consumer inference, lay belief formation, and health-related decision making while offering practical insights for marketers and policymakers navigating emerging categories such as adaptogens and psychoactives.

title: Evaluating ESCO Skill Classifiers
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Evaluating ESCO Skill Classifiers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest to declare
declarations.funderStatement: No funder to declare

detail.abstract: We present a method for evaluating ESCO skill classifiers that addresses two key challenges: the large number of skills (≈14,000) and class imbalance in the skill data. We apply this method to three different classifiers we developed, each of which analyses job advertisement text to identify required skills. Our evaluation approach uses matrix sampling of skills and job ads, incorporating clustering and stratification, and employs bootstrapping to estimate standard errors when comparing classifiers. The results show that the primary challenge for skill classifiers—whether based on text matching or large language models—is identifying all relevant skills in job ads (i.e., minimizing false negatives), rather than avoiding incorrect skill predictions (false positives). We also find that different classifiers tend to detect different sets of skills, and that text-matching methods have a good level of performance, even relative to large language models.

title: What Advertising Techniques Increase Stated Preference for Microtransit: An Application of a New Estimation Technique
affiliations: , University of Nebraska at Omaha and Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

detail.title: What Advertising Techniques Increase Stated Preference for Microtransit: An Application of a New Estimation Technique

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was reviewed and approved by our institution's Institutional Review Board.

detail.abstract: Microtransit is a form of responsive transit options (e.g., vans, minibuses) that connect transit customers to the main components of the network (e.g., scheduled bus lines, rail). The promise of microtransit in the United States and Canada is that it could connect otherwise disconnected parts of the city (e.g., low density suburbs) to the transit network thereby expanding the transit user base. However, expanding the user base to areas (and people) that traditionally have had a low propensity to use transit involves more than a connecting to the system: It requires effective advertising. We have ran a randomized trial testing the effectiveness of social and financial advertising messages. We find that while both are more effective than a baseline ad, the financial advertising message is the most effective. To do this, we have expanded the statistical technique proposed in Smith and Wooten (2023) and Smith and Wooten (2024) such that it can be used with survey data with censoring on both the top and bottom box, a common problem in Likert scale data.

title: Pre-Ordering in the Fashion Industry -Consumer Preference of the Sustainability Strategy
affiliations: ISM International School of Management, International School of Management and International School of Management

detail.title: Pre-Ordering in the Fashion Industry -Consumer Preference of the Sustainability Strategy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding has been received.

detail.abstract: The aim of this study is to empirically examine pre-ordering as a sustainability strategy in the fashion industry, measure customer preferences, and derive recommendations for action for fashion brands. To this end, two central research questions were studied in a mixed-method design: How can preordering be designed in the fashion industry to optimally meet consumer needs and achieve the highest possible willingness to buy? and "How can pre-ordering be integrated economically, sustainably, and effectively into the sustainability strategy and existing supply chains of a fashion company?" An empirical study combining qualitative expert interviews with a quantitative choice experiment are used to elicit answers to these questions. The results show that many consumers are not yet familiar with pre-ordering, but are open to it. A good price-performance ratio, high-quality materials, and high quality are crucial for greater acceptance. The biggest obstacles are uncertainties regarding fit and material, as well as long waiting times. When pre-ordering, consumers prefer basic clothing in the midprice segment with a waiting time of a maximum of two to four weeks. While sustainability awareness and fashion affinity increase acceptance, age, gender, and income have no significant influence.

title: Social Media Optimization (SMO) to Improve Islamic Banks' Marketing

detail.title: Social Media Optimization (SMO) to Improve Islamic Banks' Marketing
detail.abstract: Social media nowadays has a really great role in online marketing. Not only to advertise the product of the company, but also to get more personal with the customer. Companies or in this case, Islamic Banks, are eager to get more customers by using social media. But is the usage of social media already efficient? Has it already seize the right target market? The purpose of this paper is to share ideas on how to optimize social media to reach the target market more efficiently. Because to seize the right customer segments, not only the right social media is needed, but also the right timing and the right content of social media are needed. The study performed, based on public data analysis, and online survey results. To conclude, Islamic Banks in Indonesia can optimize their social media further, in order to reach the target market more efficiently.

title: The VoC Intelligence Transformation: Modeling the Mediating Roles of Actionability and Responsiveness in Linking Emotional Data to Service Outcomes

detail.title: The VoC Intelligence Transformation: Modeling the Mediating Roles of Actionability and Responsiveness in Linking Emotional Data to Service Outcomes

publicationDetails.detailsText: Chinese Space Science and Technology Journal, Volume 21 Issue 11, November 2025. Available Online at: www.zgkjcast-cn.linkpc.net

detail.abstract: Contemporary service organizations increasingly leverage Voice of Customer (VoC) intelligence, often derived from text analytics of natural language data, to capture customer emotion and effort. While the collection of this data-Sentiment Score (SS), Emotion Intensity (EI), and Customer Effort Score (CES)-is widespread, a significant gap remains in understanding the organizational mechanisms that successfully translate these insights into tangible service performance improvements. This study develops and tests a comprehensive VoC Intelligence Transformation (VoCIT) framework. We hypothesize that the effect of emotional and effort data on final service outcomes (Service Quality Improvement, CSAT, NPS, and Customer Retention) is not direct, but sequentially mediated by Service Recovery Responsiveness (SRR) at the operational level and Managerial Actionability (MA) at the strategic level. Furthermore, we examine the moderating effects of Service Complexity (SC) and organizational Digital Maturity (DM) on the path from insights to action. Utilizing a hybrid dataset integrating NLP-derived constructs with CRM and survey data, this research employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to validate the framework. The findings offer critical managerial implications, demonstrating that achieving service excellence through VoC is contingent upon systematic organizational alignment and the strategic prioritization of both fast recovery and sustainable managerial change.

title: Understanding Consumption
affiliations: BML Munjal University

detail.title: Understanding Consumption

keywords: Consumer behaviour Socialisation Born to shop Fast fashion E-commerce Social media influence Identity and consumption Gender and shopping Cultural norms Capitalism Shopping practices Consumption patterns Mixed-methods research Survey analysis In-depth interviews Demographic factors Media exposure Motivations for consumption Behavioural patterns Contemporary consumer culture

detail.abstract: This study examines whether contemporary consumption patterns are a result of natural human tendencies captured by the popular notion of being "born to shop"or whether they are primarily shaped through processes of socialisation. In an era defined by fast fashion, e-commerce convenience, and the pervasive influence of social media, consumer behaviour appears increasingly complex and socially constructed. To investigate the extent to which identity, gender, media exposure, culture, and capitalist structures influence shopping practices, a mixed-methods approach was adopted. A survey was conducted with 35 respondents using Google Forms, comprising 14 questions that included demographic indicators such as age, occupation, and income bracket.

title: Enhancing IT Capstone Programs through Agile Practices: Insights from Filipino Community Projects
affiliations: University of Asia and the Pacific

detail.title: Enhancing IT Capstone Programs through Agile Practices: Insights from Filipino Community Projects
detail.abstract: The IT Capstone Program at the University of Asia and the Pacific (UA&P) integrates Agile methodology through the Scrum framework to provide students with practical experiences in consultancy and software development. To extend its impact, the program was later expanded through the UA&P Filipino Community Extension Program, which engages partner communities facing challenges that require ITbased solutions. This study examines the program's implementation and areas for improvement after several years of practice. Data were collected through focus group discussions with alumni, industry practitioners, capstone students, and faculty advisers. Findings highlight the need for enhancements in sprint planning, code quality, and software maintainability to strengthen alignment with industry standards. Moreover, the study reveals how contextual factors in the adopted communities-such as IT infrastructure and government funding-affect the sustainability and effectiveness of capstone-developed solutions. The insights offer implications for refining capstone programs that aim to bridge academic training, industry expectations, and community service.

title: Cross-Return, Showrooming, and Online-Offline Competition
affiliations: , Fordham University - Gabelli School of Business, University of Washington - Foster School of Business and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Cross-Return, Showrooming, and Online-Offline Competition
detail.abstract: Nowadays, physical retailers like Kohl's and Staples allow consumers to return online purchases from etailers such as Amazon.com through their brick-and-mortar stores. This study develops a game-theoretical model to examine how such a return partnership affects demand-side competition between a physical retailer and an e-tailer. We show that, under certain market conditions, the partnership can soften price competition between the two retailers and lead to mutual profit gains. Perhaps interestingly, this outcome arises when the physical retailer is moderately inefficient in handling the e-tailer's returns and when consumers face a relatively high cost of visiting the physical retailer's storefront. In these cases, the e-tailer may strategically propose a return partnership contract that enables both retailers to coordinate their retail prices to eliminate consumer showrooming-a behavior that otherwise intensifies the competition. Finally, we find that although the partnership offers consumers an additional channel for returning online purchases, it can ultimately reduce consumer surplus due to the resulting higher retail prices.

title: The Infrastructure of Trust: A Framework for the Intelligence Age
affiliations: Patient Protect

detail.title: The Infrastructure of Trust: A Framework for the Intelligence Age

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest that could have influenced the preparation of this study. The research reflects independent analysis and synthesis conducted through Null Ventures Research without external bias or sponsorship influence.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental interventions. The analysis draws exclusively on publicly available data sources, literature review, and conceptual modeling; therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded through Null Ventures, an independent research and venture development organization. No external grants, institutional funding, or corporate sponsorships were received for this work.

keywords: structural trust JEL Codes: D82 (Asymmetric and Private Information)

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems scale in capability and deployment, they expose a fundamental constraint: intelligence is only as reliable as the trustworthiness of its data inputs. This paper introduces trust infrastructure as the foundational architecture required for intelligent systemshuman or artificial-to operate with integrity, transparency, and alignment. Trust is treated as a structural condition: an engineering problem that can be designed, quantified, and scaled across domains. We develop a four-layer framework modeling trust as a prerequisite for intelligence: the Integrity Layer (protecting data), the Value Layer (aligning incentives), the Consent Layer (verifying choice), and the Consciousness Layer (ensuring coherent internal structure). Taken together, these layers reveal trust infrastructure as the critical bottleneck in the intelligence age-more constraining than computational power and more fundamental than algorithmic sophistication. We argue that trust infrastructure depends on three foundational principles operating across all layers: security (protection from corruption), transparency (observability of system behavior), and sovereignty (individual ownership and control). Where security prevents unauthorized access, transparency enables verification, and sovereignty enables agency. Together, they transform trust from institutional faith into verifiable structure. On this basis, we outline Trust Systems Design as an interdisciplinary field bridging cybersecurity, data ethics, behavioral economics, and AI alignment. We examine implementations across domains-from healthcare data security to synthetic media authentication, digital advertising consent, enterprise data architecture, and individual data sovereignty-demonstrating that each layer can be operationalized in practice. The future, we argue, belongs not to whoever builds the largest models, but to whoever builds the most reliable foundations for them.

title: The Double Helix of Semantic Curvature: A Falsifiable Framework for Measuring Coherence in Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: The Double Helix of Semantic Curvature: A Falsifiable Framework for Measuring Coherence in Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: We introduce the double helix of semantic curvature, a geometric framework for quantifying coherence in language model outputs through paired dynamical measurements. Drawing on differential geometry, network theory, and the physics of self-organizing systems, we define response curvature (κ_prompt) and discourse curvature (κ_graph), whose lagged differential Δκ(t) reveals fundamental dynamics of semantic self-organization. We formalize three empirically testable claims: (1) stable semantic processes exhibit goldenratio (φ ≈ 1.618) convergence in both first-and second-order curvature differentials (metagolden convergence); (2) relator chain lengths in coherent discourse graphs are significantly enriched at Fibonacci indices relative to degree-preserving random baselines; and (3) semantic breakdown manifests as simultaneous connectivity spikes, curvature stagnation, and entropy production drops (spiral collapse). These criteria constitute the HG-1 Acceptance Gate, a falsifiable quality threshold with explicit failure modes. We present a production-ready implementation (kappa_helix.py v2.2.3, 2,000+ lines, 96.5% test coverage) and empirical validation protocol (HG1-EXP-01) designed to test 300 outputs from GPT-4, Claude Sonnet, and Gemini against human coherence ratings. We discuss implications for AI safety, interpretability, and the foundations of semantic physics as a quantitative science.

title: Knowledge Sharing in Modern Organizations: Barriers, Enablers, and Solutions in the Digital and Remote-Work Era
affiliations: Misr American College, Ain Shams University, Elsewedy Electric and Zadna KSA

detail.title: Knowledge Sharing in Modern Organizations: Barriers, Enablers, and Solutions in the Digital and Remote-Work Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare. This paper is a literature review and does not involve any primary data collection, commercial interests, or external influences.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it is a literature review and does not involve human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
In the contemporary knowledge economy, effective knowledge sharing (KS) is a critical driver of competitive advantage, innovation, and operational performance. This integrated literature review synthesizes findings from 22 seminal studies (2010-2025) to analyze the persistent barriers and pivotal enablers of KS, with a specific focus on the challenges precipitated by digital transformation and the remote-work revolution. The analysis reveals that while technological infrastructure is a necessary condition for KS, sociocultural and behavioral factors—such as trust, psychological safety, and a collaborative culture—are the most significant determinants of success. The paper culminates in a set of integrated, socio-technical recommendations for practitioners, emphasizing that synergistic alignment between culture, technology, and human resource systems is
essential for fostering a resilient and innovative knowledge-sharing organization.

title: From Worker to Citizen: Sculpting Reality in the Post-Truth Society
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka

detail.title: From Worker to Citizen: Sculpting Reality in the Post-Truth Society
detail.abstract:
What if your information streams were no longer shared, but generated just for you? Imagine a feed that, instead of recommending content, creates it—synthetic media produced in real time to mirror your beliefs and emotions. These bespoke realities are the accelerant for the post-truth society, fuelling the fragmentation of our shared experience and isolating each of us within our own constructed world. 

This paper argues that the socio-technical perspective, originally developed for the workplace, is inadequate for understanding this shift. We extend socio-technical systems (STS) theory beyond organisational boundaries through two new constructs—the Personal Information System (PIS) and the Societal Information System (SIS)—and introduce the Citizen Knowledge Sculptor (CKS) as a new role for navigating them. 

By mapping STS principles onto this expanded framework, we identify the competencies required for epistemic agency in a world of synthetic realities and reveal a new digital divide based not on access, but on critical literacy. This framework offers IS researchers a foundation for designing interventions that promote epistemic resilience and help restore shared truth in an era of bespoke realities.

title: Digital Enterprise Collaboration Platforms - An Interdisciplinary Progress Report
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Institute for Strategy, Technology and Organization (ISTO), University of the German Federal Armed Forces - Universität der Bundeswehr München, affiliation not provided to SSRN, ESSEC Business School, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management), affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Erlangen-Nuernberg - Organizational and Social Psychology

detail.title: Digital Enterprise Collaboration Platforms - An Interdisciplinary Progress Report
detail.abstract: Digital Enterprise Collaboration Platforms (ECPs) operate within an organization's boundaries, supporting knowledge sharing, communication, and teamwork. Yet, they frequently suffer from low engagement and coordination failures that can limit their ability to create value. This article analyzes behaviors and frictions on ECPs to propose design and governance improvements, drawing on organizational psychology, strategic management, and human-computer interaction within a two-step analytical framework. First, we view ECPs as technical infrastructures whose interfaces and interaction affordances shape user engagement and knowledge exchange. Second, we analyze them as proactive agents that deploy algorithmic nudges, recommendations, and adaptive feedback to sustain collaboration. Taken together, we propose a data-driven, test-based approach to ECP design and operation. Solutions that are personalized to meet the dynamic and diverse needs of employees can foster sustained user engagement. By integrating their digital and physical workspaces and by continuously adapting their ECPs to its users' granular behavioral data, organizations can create vital and resilient digital collaboration environments.

title: Unraveling the Path of Digital Transformation in MSMEs: The Interplay of Digital Readiness, AI Competence, and Policy Support on Business Sustainability

detail.title: Unraveling the Path of Digital Transformation in MSMEs: The Interplay of Digital Readiness, AI Competence, and Policy Support on Business Sustainability
detail.abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities have become strategic levers for strengthening micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in the data-driven economy. Despite growing awareness, AI adoption among MSMEs in emerging economies remains insufficient to sustain competitiveness. This study examines how AI readiness, digital learning capability, and innovation orientation influence AI-enabled business sustainability in Indonesian MSMEs, highlighting the role of policy support and digital ecosystem readiness. Using a quantitative approach with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) complemented by qualitative insights, the research provides empirical evidence that strategic digital capabilities and continuous learning enhance AI maturity and sustainable performance. The findings emphasize the need for institutional support, capability-building programs, and multistakeholder collaboration to accelerate responsible AI utilization and inclusive digital transformation among MSMEs.

title: LXA v1.0: A Framework to Embrace Agentic AI in Mobile Learning for Industry 5.0 Readiness
affiliations: S.B.Patil Institute of Management, Associate Professor, School of Business, PO BOX: 345050, MAHE, Dubai, DIAC, UAE, School of Business, MAHE, Dubai and S.B.Patil Institute of Management

detail.title: LXA v1.0: A Framework to Embrace Agentic AI in Mobile Learning for Industry 5.0 Readiness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to the design, analysis, or reporting of this study
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved expert opinion and secondary research only. No human or clinical participants were involved; therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Mobile learning is shifting from static content delivery to intelligent, human-centered ecosystems aligned with Industry 5.0. Yet many platforms remain fragmented, offering only limited personalization, weak ethical safeguards, and low adaptability. This study introduces the Learning eXperience with Agency (LXA v1.0) framework, developed to guide mobile learning toward 2030 through agentic AI. LXA v1.0 was created using a mixed-method approach. The process combined a scoping review of research published between 2015 and 2025, conceptual modeling, and a two-round Delphi study with 14 international experts. The review examined how learning management systems have developed into AI-enabled platforms while also pointing out persistent gaps in autonomy, transparency, and resilience. Feedback from experts stressed the need to design systems that are inclusive and firmly rooted in ethical values. The framework is built around four connected pillars. The agency focuses on learner control supported by AI. Ambient learning relates to context-aware experiences. Inclusion & ethics point to fair and transparent design. Resilience refers to the ability to adapt during periods of disruption. The Delphi validation produced strong agreement on clarity, feasibility, measurability, and relevance. Taken together, LXA v1.0 provides a tested roadmap for building mobile-first learning ecosystems that are advanced in technology, grounded in ethics, and prepared for the future.

title: The Impact of LLM-Generated Reviews on Recommender Systems: Textual Shifts, Performance Effects, and Strategic Platform Control
affiliations: Coller School of Management, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv University - Coller School of Management and Tel Aviv University - Faculty of Management

detail.title: The Impact of LLM-Generated Reviews on Recommender Systems: Textual Shifts, Performance Effects, and Strategic Platform Control

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We don't have any financial relationship that influenced this study

detail.abstract: The rise of generative AI technologies is reshaping content-based recommender systems (RSes), which increasingly encounter AI-generated content alongside human-authored content. This study examines how the introduction of AI-generated reviews influences RS performance and business outcomes. We analyze two distinct pathways through which AI content can enter RSes: user-centric, in which individuals use AI tools to refine their reviews, and platform-centric, in which platforms generate synthetic reviews directly from structured metadata. Using a largescale dataset of hotel reviews from TripAdvisor, we generate synthetic reviews using LLMs and evaluate their impact across the training and deployment phases of RSes. We find that AIgenerated reviews differ systematically from human-authored reviews across multiple textual dimensions. Although both user-and platform-centric AI reviews enhance RS performance relative to models without textual data, models trained on human reviews consistently achieve superior performance, underscoring the quality of authentic human data. Human-trained models generalize robustly to AI content, whereas AI-trained models underperform on both content types. Furthermore, tone-based framing strategies (encouraging, constructive, or critical) substantially enhance platform-generated review effectiveness. Our findings highlight the strategic importance of platform control in governing the generation and integration of AIgenerated reviews, ensuring that synthetic content complements recommendation robustness and sustainable business value.

title: From Fragmented Systems to Unified Management: ArchM, a Standardized Internet of Things Architecture for Smart Cities
affiliations: Federal University of Bahia (UFBA), Federal University of Bahia (UFBA), Federal University of Bahia (UFBA) and Federal University of Bahia (UFBA)

detail.title: From Fragmented Systems to Unified Management: ArchM, a Standardized Internet of Things Architecture for Smart Cities
detail.abstract: The growing proliferation of IoT devices in smart cities demands scalable, modular, and interoperable software architectures for device management. However, existing solutions often remain fragmented, hindering their effectiveness in large-scale and heterogeneous urban environments. This paper presents ArchM, a standardized and layered architecture that unifies the management of diverse IoT devices and services across smart city domains. ArchM separates operational and management concerns into functional layers, ensuring modularity, scalability, and interoperability through well-defined interfaces. It also introduces the concept of Smart Composition, which enables coordinated orchestration among distinct smart solutions. The architecture is compared with representative frameworks from the literature, emphasizing modularity, interoperability, and semantic orchestration. Furthermore, ArchM is evaluated through expert assessments based on the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) and ISO/IEC 25010 software quality attributes. Results demonstrate the robustness of its core management layers and highlight opportunities for refinement in upper layers related to analytics and user interaction, reinforcing ArchM as a unified architectural framework for IoT platform engineering in smart cities.

title: AI Influence: Mechanisms, Amplifiers, and Consequences
affiliations: Peking University, , , University of College London, Harvard University, Northeastern University and University of Washington

detail.title: AI Influence: Mechanisms, Amplifiers, and Consequences

declarations.funderStatement: We thank the Cooperative AI Foundation, Foresight Institute, UW Tsukuba NVIDIA Amazon Cross-Pacific AI Initiative, John S. and James L. Knight Foundation, and Sony Research Award for financial support.

detail.abstract: AI influence refers to AI's impact on the knowledge and values of individuals by acting as producers, mediators, and receivers of information. As a result, it impacts our collective processes of creating and spreading knowledge, forming beliefs, and reaching consensus. We argue that there are mechanisms of inconspicuous influence in AI development and deployment pipelines, which, when amplified by societal dynamics, could lead to dangerous outcomes that we may reverse by early interventions. We detail those mechanisms, amplifiers, and potential long-term consequences.

title: Flawed Scientific Philosophy and the Crisis of Modern Academia: How Misguided Epistemology Enables Institutional Error Suppression
affiliations: Shenyang Normal University

detail.title: Flawed Scientific Philosophy and the Crisis of Modern Academia: How Misguided Epistemology Enables Institutional Error Suppression
detail.abstract: Contemporary scientific publishing operates under a fundamentally flawed philosophical premise: that experimental data accumulation constitutes the essence of scientific research, and that experimental validation is the only legitimate criterion for knowledge claims. This epistemological inversion has produced a crisis in which theoretical research is systematically suppressed, error correction is institutionally prevented, and the discovery of novel problems is treated as insufficient for publication. Drawing on analysis of impedance matching theory in microwave absorption research, we demonstrate how false philosophical premises enable institutional gatekeeping mechanisms that suppress both theoretical innovation and error correction. We further present case studies showing that artificial intelligence systems, when presented with rigorous logical arguments, can recognize and correct theoretical errors-yet human-mediated peer review systematically prevents such corrections. We argue that genuine scientific reform requires abandoning the doctrine that "experimental validation is the only standard for testing theory" and replacing it with a framework in which (1) problem formulation through logical reasoning is the primary scientific act, (2) error is not catastrophic but essential to progress, (3) correction articles must receive equal visibility and credibility as original publications, and (4) institutional mechanisms must enable-not suppress-critical examination of majority-held theories. The contrast between AI's capacity for logical self-correction and human academia's resistance to error correction reveals not a limitation of artificial systems but a systemic failure of human institutional design.

title: Discovery of Technological Innovation Systems: Implications for Predicting Future Innovation
affiliations: University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management, University of Illinois and

detail.title: Discovery of Technological Innovation Systems: Implications for Predicting Future Innovation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Management Information Systems, volume 41, issue 1, 2024[10.1080/07421222.2023.2301172]

detail.abstract: In contrast with the accelerating trend of boundary-spanning (horizontal) technological innovation, the current Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) scheme applies a hierarchical (vertical) structure to innovation output in terms of patents. For this reason, we argue that the CPC can be complemented with dynamic technological innovation system (TIS) discovery through machine learning that accounts for horizontal relationships across seemingly disparate technologies. Using a design science approach, we propose a framework to discover boundary-spanning TISs by leveraging the textual information from millions of patents. We validate our framework in terms of the ability of discovered relationships to predict future innovation quantity and quality in different technology classes. Our novel TIS-based innovation metrics that leverage patenting activity in related technology classes are significantly associated with future innovation intensity in focal technologies. We conduct experiments with machine learning models to further tease out the predictive utility of our TIS discovery framework.

title: Don't Kill the Web: Strategic Channel Design for UGC Platforms in the
affiliations: , Tianjin University - College of Management and Economics and Tianjin University

detail.title: Don't Kill the Web: Strategic Channel Design for UGC Platforms in the
detail.abstract: With the proliferation of mobile technology and the substantial revenue potential of in-app purchases, user-generated content (UGC) platforms have strategically reduced website functionality to incentivize user engagement on mobile applications. However, this mobile-first strategy limits users' content access options, potentially dampening their content generation incentives and undermining platform profitability. Considering users' dual roles as consumers and createros on UGC platforms, we develop an analytical model in which the platform determines whether to introduce or maintain a webbased channel and, if so, its functional completeness. Our analysis shows that adding a web-based channel consistently enhances overall content generation (a content stimulation effect), which increases consumer surplus and can even mitigate cannibalization caused by the web-based channel, sometimes increasing app downloads. Nevertheless, a hybrid channel strategy is not universally optimal for UGC platforms. When the platform's intrinsic value is high, the hybrid-channel strategy can be more profitable only if it is costly to download and install the app. Conversely, when the platform's intrinsic value is low, the hybrid strategy is preferred only under moderate download costs, as a high download cost discourages user participation and reduces the return from web channel investment. Further, we find that, horizontal differentiation between the two channels critically shapes market outcomes under a hybrid channel strategy. Counterintuitively, when app download costs are low, greater differentiation can further enhance consumer surplus. Collectively, these findings suggest that UGC platforms should establish a web-based channel and strategically determine its functional completeness, while offering lightweight access options for users with high download costs to enhance engagement, stimulate content creation, and sustain long-term profitability.

title: Time in viable systems: The dimensions of time in the VSM
affiliations: UdeNar.

detail.title: Time in viable systems: The dimensions of time in the VSM

declarations.declarationOfInterest: the author has no conflicts to declare with the publication of this paper.

declarations.funderStatement: this paper has received no funding for its production. neither the research that produced it.

detail.abstract: To respond, the paper introduces the concept of the time of viability, defined as the total span during which a system maintains its identity, autonomy, and operational coherence. Drawing from Henri Bergson's concept of durée and Humberto Maturana's theory of autopoiesis, the article proposes a dual temporal model: experiential time, internal and subjective to the system, and operational time, used for coordination and external reference. This bidimensional view enriches Beer's work by grounding viability in qualitative, creative temporality rather than abstract metrics. Through a synthesis of cybernetics, process philosophy, and systems biology, the paper offers six propositions about viability time, including its role in adaptation, anticipation, synchronisation, memory, and systemic freedom. In doing so, it reconceptualizes organisational viability not merely as survival, but as a temporally embedded, self-defining process of identity maintenance across change. This theoretical proposal expands the VSM's explanatory power and opens practical avenues for managers to rethink how they diagnose, coordinate, and sustain viable systems over time.

title: Playing God: Human Digital Twin. A Legal Approach
affiliations: Alexandru Ioan Cuza University, Faculty of Law and Alexandru Ioan Cuza University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Playing God: Human Digital Twin. A Legal Approach
detail.abstract: Human Digital Twins (HDTs) seem futuristic, but the technology behind them is already a reality. Two elements make up HDTs technology: the real person and his or her digital counterpart/twin, as well as two-way communication between them. Furthermore, the actual surroundings and people that the twin interacts with in real life are transferred into cyberspace. A complete HDT does not exist, yet. In most cases, only certain aspects of human attributes are used in a particular context for specific purposes. But the technology will be able, sooner or later, to "create" a "full" HDT. This endeavour could be equated with a God creation, if we admit that God exists. To prepare to face the future, which is already here, everybody should be at least well informed. Therefore, in this article we will try to depict a comprehensible portrait of the HDTs. We will start by making a brief presentation of what Digital Twins (DTs) and HDTs technologies mean, their functioning, and their practical applications. We will focus afterwards on the legal issues concerning HDTs in an EU legal context. We will try to clarify the applicable rules and the HDTs ownership and other possible proprietary rights, such as intellectual property ones. Last, we will name a few legal and other concerns connected with HDTs.

title: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF E-COMMERCE PLATFORMS ON MARKET ACCESS OF INFORMAL ENTERPRISES IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES (2006-2025)
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business, Njala University, Indonesian International Islamic University, Students and University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) - Chengdu College

detail.title: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF E-COMMERCE PLATFORMS ON MARKET ACCESS OF INFORMAL ENTERPRISES IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES (2006-2025)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest regarding this publication
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable

detail.abstract: The objective of this study is to examine e-commerce platforms on market access for informal enterprises in developing countries from 2006 to 2025. The existing literature on e-commerce and informal economies is characterised by fragmentation and a lack of systematic, quantitative analysis that integrates these related fields. To address this gap, a bibliometric analysis was performed utilising data obtained from the Web of Science Core Collection (2006-2025). The findings reveal a steady growth in academic output, although contributions remain concentrated in a small number of countries. It also finds that most common themes are digital transformation, innovation and technology integration. The results indicate that e-commerce platforms are becoming increasingly recognised as ways for informal businesses to get access to markets. However, differences in digital infrastructure and academic representation show that growth and awareness are not always equal. The study recommends increased investment in digital infrastructure and the introduction of streamlined regulations by governments. Development partners and donors are encouraged to promote inclusive digital policies, while targeted capacity-building initiatives are necessary to empower informal enterprise owners and employees. Finally, the study calls for researchers in Africa, Latin America, and other developing countries to conduct context-specific empirical investigations to address research gaps identified in comparison with other findings from developed countries.

title: Incentivizing Drivers’ Participation During Surge Periods in Ride-hailing Platforms: Evidence from a Prepayment Program
affiliations: Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Incentivizing Drivers’ Participation During Surge Periods in Ride-hailing Platforms: Evidence from a Prepayment Program
detail.abstract:
Purpose - Ride-hailing platforms confront a critical paradox: despite a global driver base exceeding 80 million, over half of ride requests during surge periods remain unfulfilled, highlighting the contradiction between expanding supply and persistent peak-time shortages. Conventional monetary incentives are financially burdensome and unsustainable. This study investigates whether loss aversion–based prepayment programs can effectively boost drivers’ surge participation, and how effects vary by payment level and driver type.

Design/methodology/approach - Drawing on operational data from a leading Asian ride-hailing platform—covering 8,728 drivers and 50,616 weekly observations across 4 months—a staggered difference-in-differences model is adopted. Propensity Score Matching addresses selection bias, with robustness checks ensuring reliability.

Findings - Prepayment programs significantly boost driver participation during surge periods. Notably, the prepaid amount exerts an inverted U-shaped moderating effect on participation improvement. Furthermore, this moderating effect is more pronounced for drivers with lower operational capability, uncovering important driver heterogeneity in responding to prepayment incentives.

Practical implications - These findings extend loss aversion theory application, offering valuable managerial implications. Gig platforms can integrate prepayment schemes, develop tiered prepayment levels aligned with workers’ risk preferences, and implement capability-based differentiated incentive strategies to strengthen service resilience.

Originality/value - This study is among the first to empirically validate prepayment incentives rooted in self-imposed loss within the gig economy. It extends loss aversion theory by distinguishing prepayment from traditional "pre-give and claw-back" loss framing and demonstrates its application in ride-hailing contexts. Practically, it provides actionable insights to design tiered and targeted incentive strategies, enhancing surge-period supply.
