title: Evaluate The Usage of E-government Services In Sri Lanka: A Citizen’s Perspective
affiliations: University of Kelaniya

detail.title: Evaluate The Usage of E-government Services In Sri Lanka: A Citizen’s Perspective

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study received ethics approval from University of Kelaniya, Sri Lanka

detail.abstract: Information Communication Technology (ICT) has become a key factor to decide all activities in society. It has changed the shape of organizations, societies, and services across the world. According to that, information and communication technology for public administration has led the way to e-government. It makes an easy platform for citizens to find information effectively while saving its accuracy. Sri Lankan government has introduced the "E-Sri Lanka National Development" project in the year 2005 and the Sri Lanka government web portal was the central place of the same implementation. The research was focused to identify the factors that are affecting the usage of e-government services among citizens in Sri Lanka. The main objective of the study was to identify the citizens' current usage of e-government applications in Sri Lanka. The sample of the study includes internet users of Sri Lanka and the sample consisted of 384 individuals. Both qualitative and quantitative methods have been employed in this research and data was gathered by distributing printed and online questionnaires. The result of the study shows that usage of e-government service was not at a satisfactory level and awareness of e-government service had a direct impact on its usage. Moreover, lack of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, facilitating conditions and citizens' attitudes also had a direct impact on the usage of e-government services. The study was able to identify major challenges for citizen participation in egovernment services such as the absence of proper awareness, trust, insufficient infrastructure, information literacy skills, slow internet connections and attitude based issues. In this context, the study proposes three types of suggestions which can be categorized into citizens' related suggestions, technical suggestions, and organization related suggestions. E.g.: Conducting systematic awareness programs and workshops, re-engineering e-government web portal, improve computer literacy skills and improve service quality to build positive attitudes on e-government services. Conclusively it was evident that e-government services can be further developed in the context of Sri Lanka to get the maximum utilization among citizens.

title: Mobile Nudging in Medical Debt Collection: Evidence from Field Experiments with Heterogeneous Interventions
affiliations: , University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management, Sun Yat-sen University, University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management and

detail.title: Mobile Nudging in Medical Debt Collection: Evidence from Field Experiments with Heterogeneous Interventions
detail.abstract: The growing crisis of medical debt is placing a heavy strain on healthcare finances. To address the challenge of medical debt collection from patients, we propose a Three-stage Smart Nudging (TSSN) framework through targeted text messaging interventions, which strategically integrates machine learning methodologies with behavioral nudging principles to augment the effectiveness of debt collection. We conducted a series of field studies in collaboration with a top-tier hospital to evaluate the impact of the TSSN framework. In the first stage, we conducted a field experiment to assess the average intervention effect on how mobile text messages—each framed around distinct behavioral nudging principles—affect patients’ medical debt repayment. In the second stage, we apply causal forest analyses to assess by-patient group heterogeneous treatment effects. To compare the average and the heterogeneous intervention results from both stages, we conducted another field experiment in the third stage to implement the heterogeneity-driven causal targeted nudging strategy from the second stage, achieving increased patient debt repayment rates by 7.50% compared to conventional “one-size-fits-all” debt collection nudges. Grounded in the integration of theory-driven nudging principles with machine learning–based heterogeneous interventions, this study informs actionable debt collection program design by offering an effective and scalable solution for healthcare organizations and beyond, underscoring the value of the TSSN framework.

title: How Verification Alters Cultural Signals in Employer Reviews
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: How Verification Alters Cultural Signals in Employer Reviews

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzed publicly available, anonymized online review data and did not involve direct interaction with human participants. Therefore, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted as part of academic work at the University of Maryland, College Park.

detail.abstract: Online reviews shape impressions across products and workplaces. Employer reviews combine narratives and ratings that reflect organizational culture. Glassdoor permits fully anonymous posts, while Blind requires employment verification while preserving anonymity. We ask how verification changes reviews. Evidence suggests verified reviews can be more trustworthy, yet verification can also erode authenticity when expectations are unmet. We use the Competing Values Framework, which categorizes organizational culture into four types: clan, adhocracy, hierarchy, and market. Applying a specialized cultural classification model to analyze over 300,000 ratings, we find that Blind reviews emphasize clan and hierarchy dimensions, while Glassdoor reviews skew more positive overall and highlight clan and market orientations. These findings demonstrate that verification does not remove bias but rather shifts how culture is represented across platforms. Consequently, job seekers using different platforms receive systematically different signals about workplace culture at the same organizations, affecting their application decisions and ultimate job-matching outcomes.

title: Building Africa's Trust Infrastructure: How Verifiable Identity and AI Can Unlock Nigeria's Informal Economy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Building Africa's Trust Infrastructure: How Verifiable Identity and AI Can Unlock Nigeria's Informal Economy
detail.abstract: Nigeria's informal economy, valued at $243 billion and representing 43% of GDP, remains largely excluded from formal financial systems despite employing over 80% of the workforce. This paper presents a two-layered technological framework combining blockchain-based verification and AI-powered credit assessment to enable financial inclusion at scale. Drawing on 22 sources and current policy developments, the analysis examines structural barriers to formalization-including systemic invisibility (65% of GDP poorly captured in national databases), trust deficits ($32 billion SME funding gap), and verification cost mismatches ($1-5 traditional KYC vs. required <₦1 for informal businesses). The proposed framework demonstrates how multi-signal blockchain verification (utilizing phone validation, GPS location, transaction patterns, and network trust signals) combined with AI-powered alternative credit scoring can create portable, tamper-proof business identities at economically viable costs. Unlike documentation-heavy traditional approaches, this activity-based verification model meets informal businesses where they operate-enabling proof-of-existence without formal registration certificates or financial statements. The paper evaluates Nigeria's emerging digital foundation, including the Corporate Affairs Commission's AI-powered 30-minute business registration system and NITDA's Digital Literacy for All initiative, positioning these as essential precursors to comprehensive trust infrastructure. Economic impact analysis projects potential GDP growth of $50 billion by 2030 through increased financial inclusion, enhanced productivity, broadened tax base, and improved policy planning capabilities. Policy recommendations address government regulators (national digital identity frameworks using W3C DIDs, tax incentives for digital adoption), financial institutions (alternative data infrastructure, mobile-first product design, verification standard collaboration), and technology providers (localized affordable tools, data sovereignty principles, SME incubation support). The framework offers practical implementation pathways for stakeholders seeking to integrate informal economies into digital financial systems while respecting operational realities of documentation-light, cash-based business models. This research contributes to emerging literature on blockchain applications for development economics, demonstrating how technological infrastructure can enable verified economic participation at scale across Africa's largest informal economy. The Nigerian case study provides replicable insights for similar markets facing trust deficits in informal sectors.
